title: The immune system: the defence that learns and remembers

summary.text: You catch chickenpox once, but you catch a cold again and again. Your body has two defences. The first is quick and the same every time. The second is slow on the first meeting with a germ, but it picks out a cell that fits that one germ, makes many copies, and keeps a memory. Your child plays the Key Shop to see how a body can pick a matching cell from many, and runs a town test to see why vaccinating some people protects others. They learn how a vaccine gives the slow first lesson safely, and how Sarah Nelmes's blistered hand led to the first one.
summary.art: A child's outline with a quick row of round cells at the skin on one side, and on the other side a long shelf of tiny Y-shaped keys, with one key glowing and copying itself.

intro.hook: Most children in India have a small round scar on the top of one arm. It came from one tiny injection when they were babies, and it never went away. Why would a scratch from one day in your first weeks still matter now?
intro.text: That injection was a vaccine. It showed your body a harmless piece of a germ, once, long ago. Your body is still ready for that germ today. You have not forgotten it, though you do not remember it. Your body has two defences. One is quick and works the same way every time. The other one learns, and it keeps what it learns for years. In this unit you find out how a body can learn without a teacher, and how doctors found a way to use that.
intro.art: A child's upper arm with a small round scar, and a magnifying circle showing tiny cells standing guard around it.

outcomes: I can explain the difference between the quick defence that is the same every time and the defence that learns.
I can say what an antigen and an antibody are, and why one antibody fits only one germ.
I can explain, using the Key Shop test, that the body picks a matching cell from many cells it already made.
I can explain why the second meeting with a germ is faster than the first, using memory cells.
I can explain how a vaccine teaches the body without making a child ill, and why some vaccines need more doses.
I can explain herd protection, using the town test.
I can say what an allergy is, and name something about the immune system that nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: Immunity is when your body is ready to stop a germ before it makes you ill.
terms.example: After chickenpox, most people have immunity to chickenpox for life.
terms.art: A child standing inside a glowing circle, while small green germs bounce off the edge.

terms.meaning: The quick defence you are born with. It reacts to almost any germ in the same way, within minutes or hours.
terms.example: Redness and swelling around a cut, and white blood cells eating germs.
terms.art: A red swollen cut with round white cells hurrying towards a green germ.

terms.meaning: The defence that learns. It takes days on the first meeting with a germ, fits that one germ exactly, and remembers it.
terms.example: After a measles vaccine, your body can stop measles for many years.
terms.art: A long shelf of Y-shaped keys, with one key lit up and a germ lock beside it.

terms.meaning: Any shape on a germ that your immune system can notice and react to.
terms.example: The spiky bits on the outside of a virus are antigens.
terms.art: A round virus with coloured spikes, and a circle around one spike labelled with a small tag.

terms.meaning: A tiny Y-shaped protein that fits one antigen, like a key fits one lock. Antibodies stick to germs and mark them to be removed.
terms.example: A measles antibody sticks to measles and does not stick to flu.
terms.art: A Y-shaped antibody holding on to the spike of a virus, like a hand around a handle.

terms.meaning: A white blood cell that makes antibodies. Each B cell makes only one kind of antibody.
terms.example: Your body has millions of B cells, each one ready for a different shape.
terms.art: A round cell with Y-shaped antibodies sticking out all over its surface.

terms.meaning: A white blood cell that helps run the fight. Helper T cells give orders. Killer T cells destroy body cells that a virus has taken over.
terms.example: Killer T cells find a cell with a virus hiding inside and break it open.
terms.art: A round cell touching a larger cell with a small virus inside, and a small arrow showing the larger cell breaking open.

terms.meaning: A small bean-shaped knot where immune cells meet and learn about germs. You have hundreds, in your neck, armpits and groin.
terms.example: When you have a sore throat, the lumps under your jaw are lymph nodes.
terms.art: A child's neck with a small bean-shaped lump under the jaw and a magnified circle full of crowded cells.

terms.meaning: A long-lived immune cell that stays after a fight. It remembers one germ and can act within days when that germ returns.
terms.example: A memory cell for measles stays in your body for decades.
terms.art: A small round cell resting on a shelf with a tiny picture of a germ in a speech bubble.

terms.meaning: A copy of a cell. When a B cell finds a germ it fits, it splits again and again into many copies.
terms.example: One B cell can become thousands of identical copies in a week.
terms.art: One cell splitting into two, then four, then eight, all with the same Y-shaped antibodies.

terms.meaning: A safe way to show the immune system a germ, so the slow first lesson happens before the real germ arrives.
terms.example: The polio drops and injections given to babies in India.
terms.art: A syringe and a drop, with a small harmless piece of a germ shown inside.

terms.meaning: An extra dose of a vaccine that reminds the body, so its memory is stronger or lasts longer.
terms.example: The extra tetanus dose for older children.
terms.art: A calendar with a small arrow and a second syringe, and a taller bar showing stronger memory.

terms.meaning: When enough people in a place are protected, a germ cannot easily find new people to spread to. People who cannot be vaccinated are safer too.
terms.example: A baby too young for the measles vaccine is safer when everyone around is protected.
terms.art: A crowd of people where most have a green shield and the few without shields are surrounded by protected people.

terms.meaning: When the immune system reacts strongly to something harmless, such as pollen, dust or a food, as if it were a germ.
terms.example: Sneezing and itchy eyes in a dusty season.
terms.art: A child sneezing next to flower pollen, with tiny alarm bells ringing in the nose.

terms.meaning: An old way to protect against smallpox by giving a small dose of real smallpox, to cause a mild illness. It could kill, but less often than catching smallpox naturally.
terms.example: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had her children variolated in the 1700s.
terms.art: A woman holding a child's arm while another person makes a tiny scratch.

explanations.concept: Two defences: the quick one and the one that learns
explanations.definition: Innate immunity is the quick defence you are born with. Adaptive immunity is the defence that learns each germ.
explanations.description: Your first defence is innate immunity. It includes the walls you learned about in Class 3, such as skin, tears and mucus, and the white blood cells that eat germs. It reacts within minutes or hours, and it reacts in much the same way to almost every germ. That makes it fast, but it cannot tell one germ from another very well. Your second defence is adaptive immunity. It takes about a week or more the first time, because it has to find the right cell for this one germ. But it fits that germ exactly, it grows into a large army, and it keeps a memory. Both defences matter. The quick one holds the line while the slow one gets ready.
examples: Redness and swelling around a cut is the quick defence.
Antibodies against measles after a measles vaccine is the learning defence.
A cold: the quick defence gives you a runny nose, and the learning defence clears the virus a few days later.
explanations.art: Two columns. On the left, a quick sprinter with the label minutes to hours. On the right, a slower runner carrying a notebook, with the label days, and a memory shelf.

explanations.concept: Antigens and antibodies: shapes that fit
explanations.definition: An antigen is a shape on a germ that the immune system notices. An antibody is a tiny Y-shaped protein that fits one antigen.
explanations.description: Every germ has shapes on the outside. Those shapes are antigens. An antibody is a protein that has a shape on each arm of its Y. That shape fits one antigen, as a key fits one lock. When an antibody fits, it sticks. Germs covered in antibodies cannot easily enter your cells. They also clump together, and white blood cells find them and eat them more easily. An antibody against measles will not stick to flu, because the shapes do not fit. This is why the defence that learns must make a different antibody for each different germ.
examples: The spikes of a virus are antigens.
An antibody against chickenpox sticks to chickenpox and not to a cold virus.
Antibodies sticking to bacteria make them easy for white blood cells to eat.
explanations.art: A lock-shaped spike on a virus with a Y-shaped antibody key fitting in, and a different antibody that does not fit beside it.

explanations.concept: B cells and T cells: the two kinds of learning cells
explanations.definition: B cells make antibodies. T cells help run the fight and destroy body cells that a virus has taken over.
explanations.description: The defence that learns uses two main kinds of white blood cells. B cells make antibodies, and each B cell makes only one kind. Antibodies work well against germs that float around in your blood and fluids. But a virus also hides inside your own cells, where antibodies cannot reach. For this, you have T cells. Helper T cells give orders and wake up the B cells. Killer T cells check your own cells, find the ones with a virus hiding inside, and destroy them. B cells and T cells work as a team. Neither could do the whole job alone.
examples: A B cell makes antibodies for one germ shape.
A helper T cell tells B cells to start making antibodies.
A killer T cell breaks open a cell that has a virus inside it.
explanations.art: A B cell sending out Y-shaped antibodies at free-floating germs, and a T cell touching a larger body cell that has a virus hidden inside.

explanations.concept: The body chooses a defender. It does not copy the germ.
explanations.definition: Clonal selection means that the body already has many different B cells, and a germ finds the one that fits and makes it multiply.
explanations.description: How does your body make an antibody for a germ it has never met? The answer is that it makes millions of different B cells ahead of time, each with a different antibody shape, before any germ arrives. Most never meet a matching germ. When a germ arrives, one of those B cells happens to fit its antigen. That B cell is chosen, and it splits again and again into thousands of copies. Each copy makes the same antibody. The germ did not teach the body how to make the antibody. The germ only picked out one that was already there. This idea is called clonal selection. It is natural selection, as in Darwin's idea, happening inside your body in a few days.
examples: A body holds a huge range of B cells before any germ arrives.
A germ finds the one B cell that fits and makes it multiply.
The copies make identical antibodies, and the fight turns.
explanations.art: A shelf of many B cells each with a different Y shape, a germ touching one of them, and that one splitting into a crowd.

explanations.concept: First time slow, second time fast: memory cells
explanations.definition: Memory cells are B cells and T cells that stay in the body after a fight and respond within days to the same germ.
explanations.description: The first time a germ arrives, it takes about a week or more for enough of the right B cells to build up. During that time the germ can make you ill. After the fight, most of the copies die. A few stay as memory cells, sometimes for decades. When the same germ comes back, memory cells start making antibodies within two to four days, and in much larger amounts. The germ is stopped before you feel ill. This is why you usually have chickenpox only once.
examples: Most people catch chickenpox once in their lives.
A second meeting with measles is usually stopped before it causes illness.
Colds keep coming back because there are more than 200 different viruses that cause them.
explanations.art: A graph with two lines of antibody amounts over days. The first line rises slowly and low. The second line rises quickly and high.

explanations.concept: Lymph nodes: where cells meet and learn
explanations.definition: Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped organs where immune cells meet germ pieces and multiply.
explanations.description: Fluid called lymph drains from all over your body, carrying bits of whatever is in your tissues. It flows through lymph nodes before it returns to your blood. Inside the nodes, T cells and B cells wait. Scout cells from the quick defence carry a piece of a germ to a node and show it to them. If a B cell fits, it starts to multiply right there. So when you have a sore throat, the nodes under your jaw fill with dividing cells and swell. They may feel sore. That is a sign the learning defence is at work.
examples: Sore, swollen lumps under the jaw during a throat infection.
Swollen lumps in the armpit after an infected cut on the hand.
Swelling that goes back down after a week or two.
explanations.art: A neck with several bean-shaped nodes joined by thin lymph tubes, with one node swollen and crowded with cells.

explanations.concept: The two defences talk to each other
explanations.definition: Scout cells of the quick defence carry germ pieces to T cells and wake the defence that learns.
explanations.description: The quick defence and the defence that learns are not separate. A scout cell, called a dendritic cell, meets a germ at a cut. It eats the germ, cuts it up, and carries a piece of it to a lymph node. There it shows the piece to T cells. When a T cell fits, it wakes up and starts the learning defence. So the quick defence often starts the slow one. If the quick defence stops a germ at the skin, the slow one may never need to wake up.
examples: A scout cell carries a piece of a germ from a cut to a lymph node.
A T cell that fits wakes up and tells B cells to start.
A germ stopped by tears may never reach a lymph node.
explanations.art: A scout cell at a cut holding a piece of germ, walking along a thin tube to a lymph node and showing it to a waiting T cell.

explanations.concept: How a vaccine teaches the body
explanations.definition: A vaccine shows the immune system a safe version of a germ, so memory cells are made before the real germ arrives.
explanations.description: A vaccine does the slow first lesson in advance, and does it safely. There are a few ways to do it. Some vaccines use a germ that has been weakened so that it cannot make you ill. Some use a germ that has been killed. Some use only a small piece of the germ, such as a spike. Tetanus vaccine uses a harmless form of the poison the tetanus bacteria make. Newer vaccines carry a small set of instructions, called mRNA, that tells your own cells to make one harmless spike for a short time. In every case, B cells and T cells find the antigen, the right ones multiply, and memory cells stay. A sore arm or a mild fever afterwards is the immune system at work. Serious reactions are rare.
examples: BCG, polio drops and measles vaccine use weakened germs.
Injected polio vaccine uses killed polio viruses.
Hepatitis B vaccine uses a piece of the virus, and tetanus vaccine uses a harmless form of the poison.
explanations.art: Four small syringes, each with a different picture inside: a sleepy germ, a crossed-out germ, a single spike, and a tiny curl of instructions.

explanations.concept: Why some vaccines need boosters, and why flu changes
explanations.definition: A booster is an extra dose to strengthen or extend memory. Some germs change their shape, so old memory fits them less well.
explanations.description: Memory does not last the same time for every germ. For some, one or two doses give memory for years. For others, the antibodies slowly fade, and an extra dose a few years later brings them back up. Some germs also change. Flu viruses slowly change the shapes on their outside, so last year's memory fits this year's flu less well. This is why doctors update the flu vaccine. The common cold is caused by hundreds of different viruses. You may have a memory for one of them and meet a different one next month. Germs change by a kind of natural selection too. The ones whose shapes slip past our memory spread best.
examples: An extra tetanus dose for older children.
A new flu vaccine each year.
Many different cold viruses, so many colds.
explanations.art: A row of flu virus pictures with slightly different spikes each year, and a memory key that fits the first one well and the later ones less well.

explanations.concept: Herd protection: protecting people who cannot be protected
explanations.definition: When enough people in a community are immune, a germ cannot spread easily, and people who are not immune are safer too.
explanations.description: A germ needs a path from person to person. When most people are immune, the germ reaches a protected person and stops. That cuts the path to the few who are not protected. Some people cannot be vaccinated safely, such as tiny babies or people whose immune system is weak from an illness or treatment. They are protected by the people around them. How many people must be immune depends on how easily the germ spreads. Measles spreads very easily, so about nineteen in every twenty people need to be immune. A germ that spreads less easily needs a smaller share.
examples: A school where almost every child is vaccinated against measles.
A newborn baby kept safe by the people around her.
A town where a germ dies out after reaching only a few people.
explanations.art: A grid of houses where most are green-shielded, and a few unshielded houses in between, with a red germ trail stopping at the shields.

explanations.definition: A mother passes some of her antibodies to her baby before birth and through her first milk.
explanations.description: A newborn baby has not had time to build memory. So a mother lends her baby some of her own antibodies. They cross to the baby before birth. More come in the first milk, called colostrum, and in breast milk afterwards. These borrowed antibodies protect the baby for the first months. Then they slowly fade, and that is when the baby's vaccines start to matter. So the baby is first protected by her mother's memory and later by her own.
examples: A newborn who is protected from some illnesses in the first months.
Colostrum, the thick first milk, rich in antibodies.
The vaccine schedule starting just as borrowed antibodies fade.
explanations.art: A mother and a baby, with small Y-shaped antibodies drifting from the mother to the baby along a thin line.

explanations.concept: When the defence goes wrong: allergies and more
explanations.definition: An allergy is when the immune system reacts strongly to something harmless, such as pollen or a food.
explanations.description: The learning defence can make mistakes. In an allergy, it treats a harmless thing as a germ. The body makes a large reaction to pollen, dust, or a food such as groundnuts. That is why a person with an allergy sneezes, itches or gets a rash. A strong allergic reaction can be dangerous, and it needs a doctor. In some illnesses, the defence attacks the body's own cells by mistake. And in some people, parts of the defence are missing or weak. Doctors can help with all of these. Scientists are still working out why the defence goes wrong in some people and not in others.
examples: Sneezing in a dusty season.
A rash after a food that does not suit one person.
A person whose body attacks its own insulin cells, as in type 1 diabetes.
explanations.art: A child sneezing beside a flower, with a tiny alarm bell ringing in the nose and a thought bubble showing a harmless pollen grain wearing a germ mask.

explanations.concept: Down to the genes: how a body makes billions of shapes
explanations.definition: Your B cells build their antibody genes by picking pieces at random from lists and joining them, so a few hundred pieces can make billions of shapes.
explanations.description: You have only about 20,000 genes, yet your B cells can make billions of different antibodies. How? The gene for an antibody is not read from one place. Each new B cell picks one piece from each of three short lists and joins them. Then the cell adds a few random letters at the joins. Think of making a word by choosing one syllable from each of three bags. With ten syllables in each bag, you can make a thousand different words. Add random letters at the joins, and the number grows much larger. The Japanese scientist Susumu Tonegawa showed this shuffling in the 1970s, and won a Nobel Prize for it in 1987.
examples: Three bags of ten syllables give a thousand words.
Each B cell shuffles in its own random way.
Billions of shapes come from a few hundred pieces.
explanations.art: Three bags of coloured pieces, with one piece picked from each and joined in a row to make a Y-shaped antibody.

explanations.description: Scientists have learned a great deal about the immune system, but many big questions are still open. Why do some memories last for life and others fade after a few years? Why does the same germ make one person very ill and another person hardly ill at all? Why does the defence turn on the body's own cells in some people? How do the nervous system and the immune system talk to each other? These questions matter for medicine, because answers could help design better vaccines, and cures for allergies and illnesses where the defence attacks the body.
examples: How long a memory lasts for each germ.
Why a germ affects people so differently.
Why a few people's defences attack their own bodies.

perspectives.explanation: The big picture is clear, but many details of memory and of misfiring are still being worked out.

perspectives.who: Researchers on the body's wider messaging
perspectives.explanation: The immune system may be better understood as one part of a whole body of signals, linked to sleep, stress and the gut, not a separate army.

explanations.art: A large question mark above a shelf of Y-shaped keys, with a few keys lit and many keys dark.

agreed.text: The body has two defences: an innate one that reacts quickly and the same way to most germs, and an adaptive one that learns each germ and remembers it.
agreed.evidence: People and animals with a damaged adaptive defence get repeated, serious infections even though their quick defence works.

agreed.text: Each B cell makes one kind of antibody, and a germ selects the matching B cell, which then multiplies. This is clonal selection.
agreed.evidence: In 1958, Gustav Nossal and Joshua Lederberg tested single cells from a rat and found that each cell made only one kind of antibody.

agreed.text: Memory cells make a second infection much faster and stronger than the first.
agreed.evidence: After vaccines and infections, blood tests show antibodies rising within days on the second exposure, against more than a week the first time.

agreed.text: Vaccines train the adaptive defence without the illness, and have saved millions of lives.
agreed.evidence: The World Health Organization declared smallpox gone from the world in 1980, after a worldwide vaccination effort.

agreed.text: When enough people are immune, a germ spreads much less, and people who are not immune are protected too.
agreed.evidence: Across many countries, measles cases fell sharply as vaccination rose, and rose again where vaccination dropped.

agreed.text: A mother's antibodies reach her baby before birth and in her first milk, and protect the baby for the first months.
agreed.evidence: Newborns have their mother's antibodies in their blood at birth, and the amounts fall over the first months.

agreed.text: Some germs, such as flu viruses, change their outer shapes over time, so memory must be updated.
agreed.evidence: Flu vaccines are reviewed and updated every year using samples of the viruses that are going around.

challenging.claim: A vaccine gives you the disease.
challenging.who: Some worried families, and some rumours
challenging.for: Some people do get a sore arm or a mild fever after a vaccine, which can look like a weak form of the illness. A few vaccines use a weakened germ, and the idea sounds as if it carries risk.
challenging.against: Vaccines use weakened, killed or partial germs, or instructions for one harmless piece. A sore arm or low fever is the immune system at work. Serious harm is rare, and far rarer than harm from the disease.

challenging.claim: Catching the illness is always better than a vaccine, because it gives stronger memory.
challenging.who: Some families and some old sayings
challenging.for: For some germs, getting the real illness does give strong memory, and some people stayed well after illness in the past.
challenging.against: The real illness can kill or leave harm. Measles can damage the brain. Polio can paralyse. A vaccine gives the memory without that risk, and for many germs the memory lasts well.

challenging.claim: Many vaccines at once overload a baby's immune system.
challenging.for: It is natural to worry when a small baby gets several injections.
challenging.against: A baby's immune system meets thousands of germs every day. Scientists estimated, in a paper in 2002, that a baby could in theory respond to many thousands of vaccines at once. The few vaccines in the schedule use only a tiny part of that ability.

challenging.claim: You can boost your immune system with the right food, drink or pill.
challenging.who: Many adverts and some wellness books
challenging.for: Sleep, a varied diet, exercise and not smoking all help the immune system work well.
challenging.against: A stronger immune system is not always better. An overactive one causes allergies and attacks the body. There is no pill that safely makes it stronger. Sleep, food and exercise help it stay in balance.

challenging.claim: Antibodies are shaped around the germ, like clay pressed around a coin.
challenging.who: Many scientists in the 1930s and 1940s, including Linus Pauling
challenging.for: It explained how one body could make an antibody for almost any germ, even a made-in-a-lab chemical never seen before.
challenging.against: Single cells were found to make only one kind of antibody before meeting any germ. The germ selects a ready-made cell. It does not shape the antibody.

challenging.claim: Too much cleanliness in childhood weakens the immune system.
challenging.for: Allergies are more common in cleaner places, and children who grow up around animals and farms seem to have fewer. The idea is called the hygiene hypothesis.
challenging.against: The evidence is mixed. Washing hands still stops serious illnesses. Scientists think what matters is meeting a wide range of friendly microbes, not skipping hygiene.

big_questions.q: Your body made defenders for germs that have never existed on Earth, before any germ arrived. Is that planning, or is it just a very large lottery?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Key Shop test. Did anyone plan which key would fit?

big_questions.q: The first test of the first vaccine was on an eight-year-old boy. It worked, but would it be allowed today? Who should decide, and how?
big_questions.hint: Think about what Jenner knew, what he did not know, and what we require now.

big_questions.q: If you protect yourself with a vaccine, you also protect people you will never meet. Does that change who a vaccine is for?
big_questions.hint: Think about the town test. Who was safer in the town that had many shields?

big_questions.q: Your body stores a memory of every germ it has beaten, and you do not remember any of it. Where is the memory, if it is not in your mind?
big_questions.hint: Think about memory cells, and what it means for a memory to live in a cell.

big_questions.q: The immune system decides what is you and what is not you, but it also lets friendly microbes live in your gut and a baby grow inside a mother. How does it know whom to allow?
big_questions.hint: Is the line between you and the world drawn by nature, or by the defence itself?

big_questions.q: Germs also change to slip past our memory. Are they trying to win, or does it just happen, as some shapes get through and spread?
big_questions.hint: Think about how selection works, in B cells and in germs.

big_questions.q: When vaccines were new, many people were afraid of them. How should we treat fear that is real, even when the evidence says the vaccine is safe?
big_questions.hint: Think about who people trust, and why they trust them.

big_questions.q: A vaccine made in a rich country might work differently in a place where children have many gut infections. How would you test that?
big_questions.hint: Think about the work of Gagandeep Kang, who studied this in India.

story.title: Blossom's Blisters
story.note: Real: Sarah Nelmes, the dairymaid; her cow Blossom; Dr Edward Jenner of Berkeley, Gloucestershire; the boy James Phipps, aged eight; the date 14 May 1796; the test with smallpox on 1 July 1796; and the saying among dairymaids that cowpox kept off smallpox. Imagined: Sarah's thoughts, her talk with Jenner, her cows' faces, and the idea about a look-alike picture. Nobody recorded what Sarah said. Jenner did not know why it worked. The reason was found about 150 years later.
text: In the spring of 1796, Sarah Nelmes was milking cows at a farm near Berkeley, a village in the west of England. She was a dairymaid. She knew every cow by touch, even in the dark.
Her favourite was a brown cow called Blossom. Blossom had a white star on her forehead and a way of kicking the bucket when the flies bothered her. Sarah loved her.

That month, Blossom came down with a sickness called cowpox. A few sores appeared on her udder. Soon, Sarah's own hand had a few angry blisters on it, where she had touched them. They were sore, and she had a little fever for a day. But then the blisters dried, and she was well again.
“Lucky,” said the older dairymaids. “Now you will never get the smallpox.”

Sarah had heard this all her life. Every dairymaid in the valley said it. Smallpox was the worst sickness in England. It left some people dead and many more with pitted faces, or blind. Sarah's own mother had the marks all over her cheeks. Yet the girls who milked cows seemed to be spared.
One morning, the village doctor, Dr Edward Jenner, came to the farm. He was a quiet man with sharp eyes. He had heard the saying many times too, and for years he had wondered whether it was true.
“May I look at your hand, Sarah?” he asked.
He looked at the blisters for a long time. Then he asked if he could take a little of the clear liquid from them. Sarah said yes. It was the fourteenth of May.
“Why?” she asked, as he carefully touched a small glass to the blister.
“I want to see whether the cowpox really keeps off the smallpox,” said Jenner. “I shall give it to a healthy boy, and later, I shall give him the smallpox itself.”
Sarah stared at him. “On purpose?”
“On purpose,” he said slowly. “And I am not sure I should. But if I am right, it could save many lives.”

The boy was James Phipps, who was eight. He was the son of Jenner's gardener. James rolled up his sleeve and held out his arm. Jenner made two small scratches on it and pressed in the liquid from Sarah's hand. James winced and then grinned.
Sarah went back to her cows. But she could not stop thinking about it.
“Why should a cow's sickness stop a person's sickness?” she asked Blossom as she milked. Blossom flicked her tail. “They are two different sicknesses.”
She turned it over all that week. And then, one evening, she thought of something.

There were two cows at the farm that looked almost alike. Blossom and her sister, Primrose, were both brown, and both had a star on their foreheads. Strangers could not tell them apart. Sarah could, but only by the notch in Primrose's ear. If Sarah had only ever met Primrose, she would still stop Blossom at the gate and say, “Hello, Primrose.” She would be nearly right.

Sarah put down the pail. “That's it,” she whispered. “The body must keep a picture of every sickness it has beaten. Then it knows that sickness next time. And cowpox and smallpox must look nearly alike. So the picture of one nearly fits the other.”
She laughed out loud. Nobody was listening but the cows.
A week went by. James grew a little hot, and his arm was sore. Dr Jenner came every day to look at him. By the ninth day, James was running about again.
Then, on the first of July, Jenner did the thing that Sarah dreaded. He gave James real smallpox, from a person who was ill, to see what would happen.
All the village waited. Sarah milked the cows with her heart in her throat.
A day passed. Then two. Then a week. James stayed perfectly well.
Jenner came to the farm, and he was smiling. “Nothing, Sarah. Not a spot. The cowpox kept him safe.”
“Do you know why?” she asked.
He shook his head. “I do not. Nobody does. Perhaps one day someone will.”
Sarah wanted to tell him about the cows. But she said only, “Perhaps it is a kind of memory.”

Jenner looked at her for a long moment. He did not write it down. But he did write down the rest, in a book that two years later made the doctor famous. In it, he called cowpox by a Latin name that includes the word vacca, which means cow. That is where our word vaccine comes from.
Sarah's name was in the book too. It was on the page about the blisters. It was written there as Sarah Nelmes, a dairymaid. That was all it said.

She never learned what the memory was made of. Neither did Jenner. It took people another one hundred and fifty years to find the cells that keep it. But Sarah had been right about the main thing. The body does keep a picture. And a look-alike can borrow it.
story.epiphany: The body keeps a picture of every sickness it beats. Cowpox looks so much like smallpox that the same picture nearly fits both.
ask: Sarah thought a look-alike could borrow a body's memory. How could you test that idea with the Key Shop game?
Jenner was not sure he should try the test on James. What would you want to know before you said yes?
Sarah's name is in the book, but only as a dairymaid. Whose names do we forget when we tell the story of an invention?

A hand with a few blisters held out to a doctor in a dark coat, who holds a small glass.
Two brown cows with white stars side by side at a gate, one with a small notch in her ear.
A young boy rolling up his sleeve, a doctor's hands, and a woman in an apron watching from the doorway.

roots.context: We have seen how a body can answer a germ it has never met. Now we ask what that tells us about learning, about the self, and about the world we live in.

deep_truth.truth: Your body does not learn about a germ by being taught. It makes millions of kinds of defenders before any germ arrives. The germ finds the one that fits, and that one multiplies. So some learning is a choosing from what was already there.
deep_truth.habit: We think learning means being shown the answer, from a teacher to a pupil. The immune system learns another way: all the possible answers are made first, and the world picks the one that fits.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Key Shop test, nobody shaped a key for the germ. The germ simply matched one of many random keys. The more shapes were possible, the more keys we needed. In 1958, single cells were found to make only one kind of antibody each before meeting any germ.

three.who_am_i: Your body carries defenders for germs that have not been born yet. You are partly a library you have never read.
three.what_is_life: A living being holds many answers in advance and lets the world choose among them. This is how a body learns, and how living things change over many lifetimes.
three.what_is_this_world: Germs and bodies change each other. When a body gets better at stopping a germ, the germs that slip past spread best. Neither side ever finishes.

roots.thread: Before any germ arrives, your body makes billions of different shapes by shuffling a few hundred pieces. Each B cell holds one shape. When a germ fits one of them, that cell splits into a crowd of identical cells. So one set of genes holds endless possibility, and each meeting with the world brings one real thing out of it. This is the One and the many in a body: one source, many forms, and the world choosing among them.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859), chapter 4
teachings.teaching: Darwin wrote that nature does not design a living thing. Many different living things are born, and nature keeps the ones that fit their surroundings.
teachings.link: Inside your body, clonal selection does what Darwin described for whole species. Many B cells exist, the germ keeps the one that fits, and that one multiplies.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, as told in the Huayan tradition (Indra's net)
teachings.teaching: Imagine a net with a jewel at every knot. Each jewel shows a reflection of every other jewel. Nothing stands alone.
teachings.link: Your B cells together hold a reflection of every shape a germ could have. The body is a net of mirrors for a world it has not yet met.

teachings.teaching: That is whole, this is whole. From the whole the whole comes out. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole remains.
teachings.link: A chosen B cell splits into two complete cells, each as whole as the first. After the split, nothing is missing from either.

science.text: Clonal selection is how adaptive immunity works. Each B cell carries one antibody shape, a matching germ selects it, and the cell multiplies.
How long the memory of each germ lasts, and why some memories last for life, is not yet fully understood.

other_view.view: B cells follow chemistry. A shape fits or it does not fit, and the cell divides when it does. They would say there is no knowing or choosing in it, only molecules, and that calling it learning is only a way of speaking.

practice.title: Find your memory scar
practice.say: Find the small round scar on the top of your upper arm. Many children in India have one, from the BCG injection. If you cannot find it, put your hand there anyway. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. Imagine the many small cells resting in your body. Imagine one of them holding a memory of a germ from long ago. Breathe out slowly. Stay still for three breaths.
practice.kid: Find the small round scar on your upper arm. If there is none, put your hand there. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. Cells in your body are resting, ready. Some hold a memory. Breathe out. Do it three times.

ask: If your body made defenders for germs that have never existed, what else might your body be ready for that you have never met?
When a B cell splits, are there two cells, or one cell in two places?
Is choosing from what was already made a kind of learning, or a different thing?
roots.art: A child sitting still, with a faint outline of a long shelf of tiny Y-shaped keys inside her chest, and one key glowing softly.

games.title: Quick or Learning? The defence verdict
games.context: This is a guessing game. Each card shows something that happens in a body. You decide whether it is the quick defence or the defence that learns.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table, with two verdict tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud, while two others each put a token face down in front of them.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token.

setup.art: Two tokens turned over together, and the reader turning the card around to show the answer on the back.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader shows the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: something that happens in a body on the front, and the verdict with the reason on the back

items.f: Redness and swelling appear around a scraped knee within an hour.
items.b: Quick defence. The body reacts within minutes to any cut, in the same way every time.

items.f: A child vaccinated at nine months has measles antibodies in her blood at five years old.
items.b: Learning defence. Memory cells and B cells made after the vaccine keep making antibodies against measles only.

items.f: Tears wash dust out of your eye.
items.b: Quick defence. Tears are always ready, and wash away anything, not one particular germ.

items.f: A white blood cell eats a bacterium at a cut within minutes.
items.b: Quick defence. White blood cells that eat germs are on guard all the time.

items.f: A newborn baby has her mother's antibodies in her blood.
items.b: Learning defence, borrowed. Her mother's learning defence made them, and passed them to her baby.

items.f: You had chickenpox once and, when you met the virus again, you stayed well.
items.b: Learning defence. Memory cells recognised the virus and acted fast, before it could make you ill.

items.f: A fever starts a few hours after a germ gets in.
items.b: Quick defence. The brain raises the body's heat soon after the quick defence sounds the alarm.

items.f: After a booster dose, memory B cells wake up and multiply.
items.b: Learning defence. A booster reminds the memory cells, so they respond faster and in greater numbers.

items.f: Sticky mucus in the nose catches dust and germs.
items.b: Quick defence. Mucus is always there, and catches whatever lands on it.

items.f: A killer T cell breaks open a body cell that has a virus hidden inside.
items.b: Learning defence. Killer T cells are trained to fit one virus shape, and find cells that show it.

items.f: The lumps under your jaw swell for a week during a sore throat.
items.b: Learning defence. B cells and T cells are dividing in the lymph nodes.

items.f: Stomach acid kills many germs in your food.
items.b: Quick defence. The acid works on almost every germ that is swallowed.

items.f: A scout cell at a cut carries a piece of germ to a lymph node.
items.b: Quick defence. It is a scout of the quick defence, but its job is to wake up the learning one.

items.f: A vaccine leaves memory cells that last for years.
items.b: Learning defence. Memory cells are made only by the defence that learns.

items.f: Your skin keeps germs out of your body.
items.b: Quick defence. The skin is a wall that is the same against all germs.

items.f: The second time a germ arrives, antibodies appear in three days, not ten.
items.b: Learning defence. Memory cells make the second response faster and bigger.

items.f: Pus forms at a cut that has germs in it.
items.b: Quick defence. Pus is mostly white blood cells that died while eating germs.

items.f: Tiny hairs in your windpipe sweep mucus and dust upwards.
items.b: Quick defence. They work all the time, and clean away whatever lands there.

items.f: A germ finds the one B cell that fits and makes it split into thousands of copies.
items.b: Learning defence. This choosing of a matching cell is clonal selection.

items.f: A helper T cell tells B cells to start making antibodies.
items.b: Learning defence. Helper T cells are part of the team that learns.

items.f: A chemical in your spit breaks open the walls of some bacteria.
items.b: Quick defence. This chemical, called lysozyme, is in saliva, tears and mucus all the time.

items.f: A blood test shows a teenager has antibodies against hepatitis B because of a vaccine.
items.b: Learning defence. The vaccine showed the body a piece of the virus, and B cells made matching antibodies.

items.f: A person had measles as a child and is still protected from it fifty years later.
items.b: Learning defence. Memory cells can last for decades.

items.f: A sneeze blows dust and germs out of your nose.
items.b: Quick defence. A sneeze is a fast reflex that clears the nose of anything that tickles it.

rules: Quick defence means the body reacts fast, to almost any germ, in the same way. Learning defence means B cells, T cells, antibodies or memory.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one verdict token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader turns the card around and reads the back. Every player whose token matches the first words on the back scores one point.
After each card, the reader's job passes to the player on the left. With two players, you swap after every card.
If you play alone, put the cards in a pile, guess, then check the back. Score a point for each right guess.
The game ends when all 24 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: These cards show things that happen in a body. Each player gets two tokens. One says Quick defence and one says Learning defence. We will guess which defence does each thing.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take two tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Quick or Learning. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: Use blunt scissors, and a grown-up helps if the cutting is slow. With one child, the child guesses and then checks the back. With 2 to 4 children, pass the reader's job round the table.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. After each one, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card four.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone else picks a token. Turn the tokens over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who got a point?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How can you tell whether a card is about the quick defence or the one that learns?
good: If it is the same for every germ, it is quick.
If it fits one germ or remembers, it is learning.
If it takes days, it is learning.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first eight cards and learn how to tell the two defences apart.

flow.do: Play the next twelve cards. Swap the reader's job after every card. Keep a tally of points on paper.
flow.say: Keep going. Remember. The quick defence is the same for any germ and works in minutes. The learning defence fits one germ, takes days the first time, and remembers.
flow.kid: Play on. The quick defence is fast and the same for every germ. The learning defence fits one germ and remembers.

ask.q: Which cards fooled you? What made them hard?
good: The scout cell one.
The lymph node one.
Some things use both defences.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last four cards. When all cards are read, add up the points. Ask the closing question.
flow.say: That was the last card. Add up your points. Here is a question. Which defence would you rather have, if you could have only one? Why?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which defence would you keep if you had only one? Why?

ask.q: Why does your body need both defences?
good: The quick one holds the line while the slow one gets ready.
The learning one is too slow on its own.
The quick one cannot remember.

flow.think: Some cards had a bit of both. Which one was that?
flow.parent: A good answer says that the quick defence works at once but cannot remember or fit one germ, and the learning defence is exact but slow the first time. They need each other.
flow.context: This is the last step of Quick or Learning. You add up the points and think about why a body needs both defences.

games.title: Shield the Town
games.context: This is a game where you and your friends try to protect a town from a germ. You choose where to put the shields, and then a die decides how the germ spreads.

setup.art: A six by six grid of squares drawn on paper, with ten green shield tokens placed on some of the squares.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a six by six board. Place ten shields on the board.

setup.art: Two dice being rolled beside a board, with a red marker on the square where the germ starts.
setup.caption: 2. Roll two dice to find where the germ starts.

setup.art: A board where red squares have spread and stopped at a wall of green shields.
setup.caption: 3. Roll the die for each neighbour. Count the sick squares at the end.

printables.title: A six by six town board, numbered with a row number 1 to 6 down the side and a column number 1 to 6 along the top
items: Draw a grid of 6 columns and 6 rows with squares about 3 centimetres wide.
Write the numbers 1 to 6 along the top and down the side.
Colour a square red when it becomes sick.

printables.title: 12 shield tokens, small green paper squares

rules: The town is a board of 36 squares. Each square is a person. The germ will start in one square, chosen by dice.
Players work together. They agree on where to place 10 shields before the germ starts. A shielded square can never get sick.
To start the germ, roll two dice, or one die twice. The first is the row and the second is the column. If that square has a shield, roll again.
The starting square is sick. It rolls one die for each of its four neighbours, above, below, left and right. A 1, 2, 3 or 4 makes the neighbour sick. A 5 or 6 keeps the neighbour well.
Every newly sick square rolls the same way for its own neighbours. A square rolls for each neighbour only once.
When no new square gets sick, count the sick squares. The town wins if 8 or fewer squares are sick.
Play it again with a new start. Players can move up to 3 shields between rounds, but they must say why. After three rounds, add up how many rounds the town won.

flow.do: Draw the board. Put out the shields. Talk together about where ten shields would block the germ best. Place them.
flow.say: This is our town. We have ten shields and no idea where the germ will start. Where should we put them? Why there?
flow.kid: Draw the board. Talk about where to put ten shields. Place them.

ask.q: Why did you choose those squares for the shields?
good: To make a wall.
To protect the middle.
To cut the town into small parts.

flow.parent: Let the children argue. A line of shields breaks the town into parts. A scattered set leaves paths. Do not give the answer. They will see it in the first round.
flow.context: This is the first step of Shield the Town. You place the shields before the germ starts.

flow.do: Roll two dice to find the start. Colour that square red. Roll one die for each neighbour, above, below, left and right. A 1, 2, 3 or 4 makes it sick. Keep going until nothing new gets sick. Count the sick squares.
flow.say: Roll the two dice for the start. Colour it red. Now roll for each neighbour. One to four, and it is sick. Five or six, and it stays well. Keep going.
flow.kid: Roll two dice for the start. Roll for each neighbour. One to four makes it sick. Colour it red.

check.q: A square next to a sick square has a shield. Can it get sick?
options: No, a shield protects it
Yes, if the die says so
Only if two neighbours are sick
check.why: A shielded square never gets sick, whatever the die says. The germ has to find another path. This is how protected people stop a germ from spreading to the people near them.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first round and watch where the germ spreads.
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, split the jobs: one rolls, one colours the sick squares, one keeps a list of squares still waiting to roll. Swap each round. A single child does all three jobs. Chance matters, so one lost round does not mean the shields were wrong.

flow.do: Count the sick squares. If 8 or fewer squares are sick, the town wins. Look at the board. Where did the germ stop? Which shields did the most good? Move up to three shields and play again.
flow.say: Count the red squares. Eight or fewer, and the town wins. Look at where the germ stopped. Which shields helped most? You may move three shields. Where will you put them?
flow.kid: Count the red squares. Eight or fewer is a win. Move up to three shields. Play again.

ask.q: Which shields did the most good, and which did none?
good: The ones that blocked a path.
The ones near where the germ started.
The ones the germ never reached did nothing.

flow.context: In this step, you score the round and change the shields.
flow.parent: With ten shields, shields scattered at random leave the town winning about half the time, and a wall of shields right across the town wins most rounds. Let the children find this by playing, and do not tell them first.

flow.do: Play one more round. Add up how many of the three rounds the town won. Then ask the closing question.
flow.say: That was the last round. How many did the town win? Here is a question. If you could not choose where the shields go, what would that mean for a real town?
flow.kid: Count your wins. What if you could not choose where the shields go?

ask.q: In a real town, we cannot choose who is protected so carefully. What does that mean for how many people we need to protect?
good: We need to protect more people.
We need many people to be protected.
It is safer if almost everyone is protected.

flow.think: In your game, a few well-placed shields did a lot. In real life, who are the people near the edge, who are safe only when others are protected?
flow.context: This is the last step of Shield the Town. You add up wins and think about real towns.

experiments.title: The Key Shop: how many random cells until one fits?
experiments.question: If a body makes defender cells with random shapes, how many does it need to make before one of them fits a new germ? Does it need more when there are more possible shapes?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many random cells will you need before one fits the germ? Will you need more cells when each cell has more flips in its code? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The germ's code is flipped once for each size of code, and it stays the same through all the rounds of that size. Every defender cell is made the same way, by flipping the same number of times. The only thing that changes between the three parts is the number of flips in the code, which is the number of shapes that are possible. That way, any difference in the number of cells needed comes from the number of shapes.

materials.item: one coin, of any kind
a pencil
2 sheets of paper
a clock or phone timer, to keep an eye on the time
a grown-up or a sibling to be the helper, if you like (with 2 to 4 children, each child is a separate body: each plays their own rounds, then you pool the numbers)

experiments.record: Write the number of cells you needed in each round (six rounds for three flips, eight for two flips, four for four flips) in the table. At the end, add the numbers in each row and divide by the number of rounds to find the average. Then say what you thought, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this test, you play a body that makes defender cells at random, and a germ that has one shape. You count how many random cells you need to make before one of them fits.

setup.art: A hand flipping a coin three times, with the results H, T, H written on a card labelled Germ.
setup.caption: 1. Flip the coin three times to give the germ a code. Write it on a card.

setup.art: A list of the eight possible codes, from HHH to TTT, written down the side of a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 2. Write all the possible codes in a list. Count how many there are.

setup.art: A hand flipping a coin three times, with the result written as a new code under a column labelled Cell 1, Cell 2, Cell 3.
setup.caption: 3. Make a defender cell. Flip three times and write its code.

setup.art: A table with rows for two, three and four flips and a number of cells needed written in each round.
setup.caption: 4. When a cell matches the germ, write how many cells it took. Start a new round.

flow.do: Read out the rules of the game. The germ has a code made of coin flips. The body makes random cells by flipping the same number of times. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Imagine a germ with a shape. We show the shape as three coin flips, like heads, tails, heads. Your body makes new defender cells with random shapes. How many random cells do you think it needs before one fits? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A germ has a shape made of three coin flips. Your body makes random cells. How many will you need before one fits? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen if each code has four flips instead of three? Why?
good: There are more shapes, so it will take more cells.
It is harder to match, so more tries.
More possible shapes, so a longer search.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the sheet. Most children guess between three and ten.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Key Shop test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Write all eight possible three-flip codes in a list: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT. Flip the coin three times for the germ, and write the code on a card. Keep the card face up.
flow.say: Here are all the shapes that a cell with three flips can have. Count them. How many are there? Now flip three times, to give the germ a shape. Write it here.
flow.kid: Write all eight three-flip codes in a list. Flip three times for the germ. Write its code on a card.

ask.q: How many different shapes are possible with three flips?
good: Eight.
Eight, because each flip has two choices and there are three flips.

flow.parent: If your child asks how to be sure of eight, list them in order, as heads then tails for each place. There are two choices for the first flip, two for the second and two for the third, so two times two times two is eight.

check.q: How many different shapes are possible if each cell has two flips?
options: Four
Six
Two
check.why: Two flips give heads or tails twice. The shapes are HH, HT, TH and TT. That is four. Each extra flip doubles the number of shapes.

flow.context: In this step, you list every possible shape and give the germ one. The list shows how many shapes the body must be ready for.

flow.do: Make a defender cell. Flip the coin three times and write the code. If it is the same as the germ, write down how many cells you have made so far. If not, make another cell. Do this for six rounds. Each round starts again at cell number one.
flow.say: Now you are the body. Make one cell at a time with three flips. Does it match the germ? If not, throw it away and make another. Count the cells. Do six rounds.
flow.kid: Flip three times. Does the code match the germ? If not, make another cell. Count how many. Do six rounds.

ask.q: Did any round take far longer than the others? What do you think happened?
good: I had bad luck.
The matching shape came up late.
It is random, so some rounds take longer.

flow.parent: Over many rounds the average is about eight, but single rounds can take from one cell to twenty or more, and the average of only six rounds can land anywhere from about 5 to 12. That is normal for chance. With siblings, each child plays six rounds, then add all the rounds together for a steadier average. If your child is tired, share the flipping, one flips and one writes. Do not stop before six rounds.

check.q: Why do we flip the coin to make each defender cell, instead of choosing the best one?
options: A real body does not know a new germ's shape in advance
Flipping is faster than choosing
The germ tells the body what shape to make
check.why: A body makes its cells before a germ arrives, so it cannot know the germ's shape. The only way is to make many random cells and hope one fits. A wrong pick often comes from thinking the body is told about the germ.

flow.context: In this step, you play the body with three flips in each code. You count how many random cells you need to make before one fits.

flow.do: Flip the coin two times and write the germ's new code. Make cells with two flips each. Count how many it takes to match. Do eight rounds, and write each number in the table.
flow.say: Now the shapes are simpler. Each cell has only two flips. There are fewer shapes to choose from. Do eight rounds and write the numbers. I wonder if you will need fewer cells.
flow.kid: Now use two flips. Make a new germ code. Do eight rounds. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Two flips give four shapes. The average is typically about four, but with eight rounds it may be anywhere from about 3 to 6. Rounds will be quick, about half a minute each.
flow.context: In this step, you try the game again with fewer possible shapes. You are checking whether the number of shapes changes how many cells you need.

flow.do: Flip the coin four times and write the germ's new code. Make cells with four flips each. Count how many it takes to match. Do four rounds. Each round may take a couple of minutes.
flow.say: Now every code has four flips. That makes more shapes. Do four rounds. It may take a while. Keep counting.
flow.kid: Now use four flips. Make a new germ code. Do four rounds. Be patient.

ask.q: While you flip, what do you notice about how long this is taking?
good: It is taking much longer.
The matching shape is harder to hit.
There are more shapes to get through.

flow.parent: Four flips give sixteen shapes. The average over many rounds is about sixteen, but with only four rounds yours can land anywhere from about 7 to 30, and single rounds may take forty cells or more. If time runs short, do two rounds and add a sibling's numbers to yours. Each cell is four flips, so use a die instead if your coin gets tiresome: odd is heads, even is tails.
flow.context: In this step, you try the game with even more possible shapes. You can see what happens to the search when the number of shapes grows.

flow.do: Add the numbers in each row and divide by the number of rounds, to find the average. Look at the three averages. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then ask the two questions below.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see in the numbers? Why do you think that happened? Then look at the three averages. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Find the average for each row. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What happened to the average each time we added one more flip to the code?
good: It about doubled.
It went up a lot.
More shapes meant more cells.

ask.q: A real body has billions of possible shapes. How could it ever find a match in time?
good: It makes lots and lots of cells.
It makes many at the same time.
It starts with many already made.

flow.think: Nobody told the germ which cell to meet. Did the body learn the germ's shape, or did it find a cell that already fitted?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that each extra flip doubled the shapes and about doubled the cells needed. The averages are typically near four, eight and sixteen, but chance can bend them, especially the four-flip row. The safe thing to look for is the order: more flips, bigger average. After they have said what they saw, explain: a body does not shape a cell for a germ. It makes huge numbers of random cells, many at once, so that some fit almost any germ. When one fits, it multiplies. If your numbers did not follow the pattern, say so. Chance can hide a pattern, and more rounds would show it.

check.q: In your results, the average number of cells rose when the code had more flips. What does this show?
options: More possible shapes means more cells are needed to find a match
A longer code makes the germ smaller
The coin gets tired
check.why: More flips give more possible shapes, and the matching one is rarer. So you need to make more random cells before one fits. A real body deals with this by making enormous numbers of cells.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Key Shop test. You find the averages and explain what the numbers show about how a body finds a matching defender.

experiments.title: Spread and Shield: does protecting some squares protect all?
experiments.question: In a small town, how many people get sick when a germ starts with one person? Does shielding some people protect the rest?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which town will have the fewest sick squares: no shields, 8 shields or 16 shields? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every town is a grid of 25 squares, and the germ always starts in the middle square. Every sick square rolls the same die in the same way for each of its neighbours. The only thing that changes is how many squares have a shield, and the shields are placed by drawing numbered slips, so nobody can pick the best places. Any difference in the number of sick squares comes from the number of shields.
results_table: Squares not shielded and still well

materials.item: 2 sheets of paper, a ruler and a pencil
a red pencil or pen, and a green pencil or pen (any two colours will do)
24 small paper slips, numbered 1 to 25 with 13 left out
a small bowl or a cup to draw the slips from
one die (from Ludo or Snakes and Ladders is fine)

experiments.record: Write the number of shields, the number of sick squares and the number of well but unshielded squares for each town. Then draw a bar for each town to show the sick squares.
experiments.context: In this test, you play a germ that spreads through a town of 25 squares. You find out how many squares get sick with no shields, with a few shields and with many shields.

setup.art: A square of paper drawn as a grid of five by five squares, numbered 1 to 25, with the middle square coloured red.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a grid of 25 squares. Colour square 13 in the middle red. It is sick.

setup.art: A hand drawing a numbered slip from a bowl, and a green shield mark being drawn on the matching square.
setup.caption: 2. Draw slips from the bowl. Mark each drawn square with a green shield.

setup.art: A die being rolled beside a red square, with arrows pointing to the four neighbours above, below, left and right.
setup.caption: 3. For each neighbour, roll the die. A 1, 2, 3 or 4 makes the neighbour sick.

setup.art: A finished grid with many red squares, a few green shields and a few untouched white squares.
setup.caption: 4. Stop when nothing new gets sick. Count the red squares.

flow.do: Show your child the three towns you will test. Town A has no shields, town B has 8, and town C has 16. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will test three towns. In town A, nobody has a shield. In town B, eight squares have shields. In town C, sixteen have shields. Which town will have the fewest sick squares? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three towns: no shields, eight shields, sixteen shields. Which gets the fewest sick squares? Why?

ask.q: If the germ cannot pass through a shield, what will it do in town C?
good: It will get stuck.
It will have to go around.
It will stop quickly.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children guess that more shields means fewer sick squares. A good question is whether the unshielded squares are safe too.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Spread and Shield test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Draw a grid of five squares by five squares, each about 3 centimetres wide. Number the squares 1 to 25, row by row. Write the numbers 1 to 25 on slips of paper, but leave out 13. Put the 24 slips in the bowl. Draw the grid three times, for towns A, B and C.
flow.say: This is your town. Each square is a person. The middle square, number 13, is the first person who is sick. Colour it red. We draw the grid three times, one for each town.
flow.kid: Draw a grid of five by five squares. Number them 1 to 25. Colour square 13 red. Draw it three times.

check.q: Why do we draw the shields from a bowl, and not choose the squares?
options: So nobody can pick the best places to block the germ
So the game takes longer
So the slips get used
check.why: If we chose where the shields go, we might block the germ's paths in a clever way. Drawing from the bowl means that only the number of shields can make a difference.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the three towns and prepare the slips. The slips decide where the shields go, so the test is fair.
flow.parent: A ruler makes this go faster. Let your child draw one grid and trace the other two, or photocopy a grid. With 2 to 4 children, each child draws one town and the slips are shared; one rolls, one colours, and the others check that no neighbour is missed.

flow.do: Play town A, which has no shields. Square 13 is sick. For each of its four neighbours, above, below, left and right, roll the die. A 1, 2, 3 or 4 makes that neighbour sick. Colour it red. Then each new red square rolls for its own neighbours, once per neighbour. Skip a neighbour that is already red. Stop when no new square gets sick. Count the red squares.
flow.say: Square 13 is sick. It rolls the die once for each neighbour. A one, two, three or four makes that neighbour sick. Colour it red. Then the new red squares roll for their neighbours too. Keep going until nothing new gets sick.
flow.kid: Square 13 rolls for each neighbour. A 1, 2, 3 or 4 makes it sick. Colour it red. Keep going.

ask.q: What path did the germ take through your town?
good: It spread outward from the middle.
It went in all directions.
It followed the squares next to each other.

flow.parent: Each sick square rolls only once for each neighbour, the moment it becomes sick. Keep a list of squares waiting to roll so none is forgotten. With no shields the germ typically reaches about sixteen to twenty-five squares. Rarely it dies out early by chance, so if it stops at a few squares, play town A again.
flow.context: In this step, you play town A with no shields. This shows how far a germ spreads when nobody is protected.

flow.do: Play town B. Draw 8 slips from the bowl. Mark those squares with a green shield. Put the slips back. Square 13 is sick. Roll for the neighbours as before, but shielded squares never get sick. Count the red squares.
flow.say: Now eight squares get a shield. Draw eight slips and mark them green. A shielded square cannot get sick, so the germ cannot pass through it. Roll as before. How many squares get sick this time?
flow.kid: Draw eight slips. Mark those squares green. Shielded squares never get sick. Roll for the germ. Count.
flow.parent: Put every slip back after drawing, so the bowl is full again for town C. Town B typically has about 2 to 14 sick squares, around 8 on average. Chance matters a lot with so few squares. If a shield lands right next to square 13, that may block much of the spread.
flow.context: In this step, you play town B with 8 shields. You can compare it with town A.

flow.do: Play town C. Draw 16 slips from the bowl. Mark those squares with a green shield. Square 13 is sick. Roll for the neighbours as before. Count the red squares. Then count the squares that are not shielded and still well.
flow.say: Now sixteen squares get a shield. Draw sixteen slips and mark them green. Roll as before. Count the sick squares. Then count the squares that have no shield and are still well.
flow.kid: Draw sixteen slips. Mark them green. Roll for the germ. Count the sick squares.

ask.q: Some squares have no shield and are still well. Why did the germ not reach them?
good: The shields around them blocked the germ.
The germ could not get to them.
They were behind the shielded squares.

flow.parent: Town C typically has only 1 to 5 sick squares, rarely up to 9. Many unshielded squares stay well. That is the idea of herd protection: the shields protect the squares around them too.
flow.context: In this step, you play town C with 16 shields. You look at the squares with no shield that stayed well.

flow.do: Write the results in the table. Draw a bar for each town to show the sick squares. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then ask about the unshielded squares that stayed well.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see in the three towns? Why do you think that happened? Look at the unshielded squares that stayed well. What protected them?
flow.kid: Write the numbers in the table. Draw a bar for each town. Say what you thought, saw and why.
flow.think: In a real town, some people cannot be vaccinated. Who protects them?

check.q: In town C, several unshielded squares stayed well. What protected them?
options: The shielded squares around them blocked the germ's paths
Unshielded squares can never get sick
The die gave them good luck
check.why: A germ can only travel from a sick square to a touching square. Shields block those paths. An unshielded square surrounded by shields has no path to it. That is how a crowd of protected people can protect the few who are not.

flow.parent: A strong answer says that more shields meant fewer sick squares, and that shields protected some unshielded squares too. Dice are random, so one run can surprise you. Town B and town C can swap places by chance, because the slips decide where the shields go. If your results do not follow the pattern, run towns B and C again with a new draw and add the results together. With siblings, each child runs their own B and C and you compare the totals. After they have said what they saw, explain: real germs differ in how easily they spread. Measles spreads very easily, so almost everyone must be protected to stop it. A germ that spreads less easily needs fewer shields.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Spread and Shield test. You compare the three towns and explain what the shields did.

activities.title: Read the vaccination card

materials.item: your family's vaccination card for your child, or any child in the family (often called the Mother and Child Protection card). With 2 to 4 children, each child brings a card, or you compare the example card with your own.
paper and a pencil
if you have no card, the example card in the first step

activities.record: Write the names of three vaccines on the card. Write how many doses of each. Draw one question you have about the card.
activities.context: In this activity, you look at a real vaccination card. You notice what is on it and what you wonder, before you learn the reasons.

setup.art: A parent and a child at a table, looking at a small booklet with a table of dates and vaccine names.
setup.caption: 1. Open the vaccination card together.

setup.art: A finger pointing at three rows in the booklet, each with the same vaccine name and several dates.
setup.caption: 2. Find a vaccine that has more than one date next to it.

setup.art: A child pulling up a sleeve to show a small round scar on the upper arm.
setup.caption: 3. Find the small round scar on the upper arm.

flow.do: Open the card to the page of vaccines. If you have no card, use this example for a girl named Kavya. Birth: BCG and hepatitis B. 6, 10 and 14 weeks: polio drops and more. 9 months: measles and rubella. 16 months: a second measles and rubella dose. 5 years: a booster. Your own card may differ. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: This card lists the vaccines a child has had. What do you notice? What do you wonder? Take your time.
flow.kid: Look at the card. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

ask.q: What do you notice about the dates and the vaccines?
good: Some vaccines appear again and again.
Most are given when the child is a baby.
There are different dates for the same vaccine.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Let your child notice. Write down what they say. The reasons come later in the unit. Cards differ by state and year. If your child's card is hard to find, ask a clinic.
flow.context: This is the first step of Read the vaccination card. You look and wonder before anything is explained.

flow.do: Ask your child to circle the vaccines that have more than one date. Count the doses of each. Write the counts on paper. Ask why they think some have more than one dose. Then count every dose on the card from birth to five years old, and write the total.
flow.say: Circle every vaccine that appears more than once. How many doses does each one have? Why do you think some have more than one?
flow.kid: Circle each vaccine with more than one date. Count the doses. Why more than one?

ask.q: Why do you think some vaccines are given more than once?
good: Maybe one dose is not enough.
The body may forget.
Maybe the second one makes it stronger.

flow.parent: Wonder is the goal here. Good guesses appear as questions: does the body forget? Does it need reminding? Keep those questions for the explanation card on boosters. The total is often around twenty doses and visits for a child to five years, but it differs by state and card. If two children have cards of different ages, compare their totals and say why they differ.
flow.context: In this step, you count the doses on the card. You notice that some vaccines come in several doses.

flow.do: Ask your child to find the small round scar on the top of one upper arm. Many Indian children have it, from the BCG vaccine. It is more often on the left arm. Not every child has one. Draw the scar in the notebook.
flow.say: Look at the top of your upper arm. Many children have a small round scar there. It is from one tiny injection when you were a baby. Why would a scar from long ago matter now?
flow.kid: Look at the top of your upper arm. Is there a small round scar? Draw it.
flow.parent: Not every child has a visible scar, and that does not mean the vaccine did not work. If there is no scar, skip the question and move on.
flow.context: In this step, you look for the scar the BCG vaccine leaves. It connects the card to your own body.

activities.title: Faster the second time: the word puzzle model

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a clock, a phone timer or a stopwatch
the six scrambled words in the first step
six new scrambled words, given in the last step

activities.record: Write the time it took the first time, the second time, and for the six new words. Draw three bars to show them. Say why the second time was faster.
activities.context: In this activity, you solve a puzzle twice. The second time is a small model for how memory cells make the second meeting with a germ faster.

setup.art: A child with a timer, bending over a sheet of six scrambled words, with a pencil in hand.
setup.caption: 1. Start the timer. Solve all six scrambled words.

setup.art: The same sheet with all words solved, and a number written below showing the time.
setup.caption: 2. Write down how long it took.

setup.art: The same sheet turned face-down, and then the child solving the same six words again with a shorter time written beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Wait a minute. Do the same six words again. Write the new time.

flow.do: Write the six scrambled words on paper: CANCIEV, ROMEMY, MREG, HPLYM, HEDLIS, LCEL. Start the timer. Your child unscrambles all six. Stop the timer when the last word is solved. Write the time.
flow.say: Here are six scrambled words. They all come from our unit. Unscramble them as fast as you can. I will time you. First, guess. Will the second time be faster or slower? Why do you think so?
