flow.kid: Unscramble six words. Your grown-up times you. Guess first. Will the second time be faster? Why?
flow.parent: The answers are VACCINE, MEMORY, GERM, LYMPH, SHIELD and CELL. Do not give hints. Any time is fine. A first time of one to three minutes is common.
flow.context: This is the first step of Faster the second time. You solve the puzzle once and write down how long it took.

flow.do: Turn the sheet over. Wait one minute. Then give your child the same six scrambled words again on a new sheet, in the same order. Start the timer. Write the time.
flow.say: Now the same six words again. Ready? Go. I will time you again.
flow.kid: Do the same six words again. Your grown-up times you.

ask.q: Why was the second time faster?
good: I remembered the answers.
I already knew them.
My brain kept them.

flow.parent: The second time is almost always much faster, often by half or more. If it is not, say so. Honest results matter.

check.q: In the puzzle, why was the second time faster?
options: You remembered the answers from the first time
The words got easier
The timer was slower
check.why: The first time, you had to search for each answer. The second time, you remembered them. A body's memory cells do something like this. The first meeting with a germ is slow, and the second is fast.

flow.context: In this step, you solve the same puzzle again and write down the new time.

flow.do: Now test whether you were only warmed up. Give your child six new scrambled words: OBDOL, SURIV, NEGE, VEREF, NOEB, KLIM. They are BLOOD, VIRUS, GENE, FEVER, BONE and MILK. Time it. Draw three bars: first try, second try and new words. Ask your child to say how the puzzle is like the body, and how it is not.
flow.say: Draw one bar for each time. How is this puzzle like what a body does the second time it meets a germ? How is it not?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each time. How is this like a body meeting a germ twice?

ask.q: How is the puzzle like your body meeting a germ a second time?
good: The second time is faster.
Memory helps.
It is quicker when you have done it before.

ask.q: How is the puzzle not like your body?
good: My brain remembered, not cells.
My body does it without thinking.
The germ is not a puzzle.

flow.think: A body keeps its memory of one germ in cells, not in a mind. What would the puzzle be like if your hands remembered, but you did not?
flow.parent: The new words will usually take about as long as the first try, or a little less. That shows the speed-up was memory of those very words, as a memory cell remembers one germ. A strong answer says the puzzle is like memory cells because the second time is faster, and the new words are slow again because memory fits one thing. It is different because the body does it with cells and chemicals, not by thinking, and the memory can last for years. With siblings, one solves while another times, and then swap roles with new words.
flow.context: This is the last step of Faster the second time. You compare the puzzle with the body, and say where the comparison stops working.

activities.title: Find your lymph nodes

materials.item: your own fingers, a mirror if you like
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Touch gently. Never press hard on the neck. If any lump is large, hard, painful for more than a few days, or lasts more than two weeks, show a doctor.
activities.record: Draw a neck with the places where you felt the nodes. Write whether they felt soft or firm, and big or small.
activities.context: In this activity, you gently look for your own lymph nodes, where the cells that learn about germs meet. You find out where to feel them when you are well.

setup.art: A child with two fingers gently touching the soft part just under the jaw on one side.
setup.caption: 1. Gently feel under your jaw with two fingers.

setup.art: A child touching just behind the ear, and then the armpit with the other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Try behind the ear and the armpit.

setup.art: A drawing of a neck with small dots marking where the nodes were felt.
setup.caption: 3. Draw where you felt them.

flow.do: Ask your child to feel gently with two fingers just under the jaw on each side. Use light, circling touches, as if feeling a small pea under the skin. Then try the sides of the neck, behind the ears, and in the armpit.
flow.say: Use two fingers. Touch very gently under your jaw. Make tiny circles. Can you feel a small bump like a pea? Many children can. Try behind your ear too.
flow.kid: Gently feel under your jaw. Make tiny circles. Is there a bump like a small pea?

ask.q: What do you notice about the bumps? Are they soft or firm? Big or small?
good: They are small.
They are soft.
They move a bit.

flow.parent: Healthy lymph nodes are small, soft, movable, and not painful. Some children can feel them easily and some cannot. Both are normal. Do not press hard. Stay with your child. With siblings, take turns and wash hands first; compare sizes using a pea or a grain of rice as a measure.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find your lymph nodes. You feel where the nodes are when you are well.

flow.do: Draw a neck and mark where the nodes were felt. Ask why they think a sore throat makes these nodes swell. If anyone at home has a sore throat or a cold, ask them if you may gently feel their jaw nodes too. Compare.
flow.say: Draw a neck. Mark where you felt the bumps. When you have a sore throat, those bumps can swell. Why do you think that happens? What could be going on inside?
flow.kid: Draw a neck. Mark the bumps. Why might they swell when you are ill?

ask.q: Why might the nodes swell during a sore throat?
good: Cells are gathering there.
Cells are fighting.
Many cells are working there.

flow.parent: Let your child guess. The explanation comes in the lymph node card: the nodes fill up with dividing B cells and T cells. If your child asks, you can say that they fill with cells that are fighting the germ.
flow.context: In this step, you draw where the nodes are and wonder why they swell when you are ill.

activities.title: Once or again? A family survey

materials.item: paper and a pencil
five people to ask, such as parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles or neighbours
coloured pencils

schedule.what: Ask five people the three questions. Write the answers in the table.
Add up the answers. Draw a bar chart. Say what you notice and why.

activities.record: Write each person's answers in a table. Draw a bar chart for each illness. Write one sentence about what you notice.
activities.context: In this activity, you ask people in your family whether they have had chickenpox, measles and colds once or more than once. You look for a pattern and wonder why.

setup.art: A child with a notebook asking an older woman a question, with a table of three illnesses drawn on the page.
setup.caption: 1. Ask five people. Write each answer in a table.

setup.art: A table with five rows of tally marks under chickenpox, measles and colds.
setup.caption: 2. Write how many times each person had each illness.

setup.art: Three bars drawn in coloured pencil, one for each illness, with different heights.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar chart. Look for a pattern.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess first. Which illness do people get most often: chickenpox, measles or a cold? Why? Write the guess. Then ask five people: have you had chickenpox? How many times? Measles? How many times? A cold? About how many in the last year? Write the answers in a table.
flow.say: We will ask five people three questions. Have they had chickenpox, and how many times? Have they had measles, and how many times? A cold, and about how many times? First, which do you think they will have had most often? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which illness do people get most? Ask five people three questions. Write the answers.

ask.q: Which illness do you think people will have had most often? Why do you think so?
good: Colds, because everyone gets them.
Colds, because they are common.
Chickenpox, because it is catching.

flow.parent: Expect colds to be a few in a year, often two to five and more for children, and chickenpox and measles to be zero or one. Some people may not remember, and some may not have had them, because they were vaccinated. Write what they say. Be kind about forgetting. With 2 to 4 children, each asks a different five people, then you add the tables together. Phone calls to relatives are fine.
flow.context: This is the first step of Once or again. You guess, and then you ask five people about their illnesses.

flow.do: Add up the answers. Draw one bar for each illness, to show the average number of times people had it. Ask your child what they notice. Ask why colds might come again and again, while chickenpox rarely does.
flow.say: Add up the answers and draw a bar for each illness. What do you notice? Why might colds come again and again while chickenpox hardly ever does?
flow.kid: Add up the answers. Draw a bar for each illness. What do you notice? Why?

ask.q: Why might you get colds again and again, but chickenpox only once?
good: Many different viruses cause colds.
The cold virus is different each time.
The body remembers chickenpox.

flow.think: If one cold virus gave you a memory for life, why would you still catch a cold next month?
flow.parent: Strong answers say that more than 200 different viruses cause colds, so a memory for one does not help against another. Chickenpox is one virus, and memory cells remember it. After they have said what they think, explain this.

check.q: A person had a cold last month and has another cold this month. Which is the best reason?
options: Different viruses cause colds, so memory for one does not fit another
The first cold made the body weaker
Cold viruses only attack the same person twice
check.why: More than 200 different viruses cause colds. Each has different shapes on the outside. A memory for one does not fit another. Colds do not make the body weaker. They just come from different viruses.

flow.context: This is the last step of Once or again. You draw the chart and think about why memory helps for some illnesses and not for others.

activities.title: Paper keys and a changing germ

materials.item: thin card or an old cereal box
scissors, a pencil and a ruler
coloured pencils

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors.
activities.record: Draw the three germs and the antibody that fits each. Draw the changed germ. Say whether the old antibody fits it.
activities.context: In this activity, you cut paper germs with different notches and paper antibody keys that fit them. Then you change a germ's shape and see what happens.

setup.art: Three pieces of card with different notches cut into one edge: a triangle, a half circle and a square.
setup.caption: 1. Cut three germs, each with a different notch.

setup.art: Three small Y-shaped pieces of card, each with a tip matching one of the notches.
setup.caption: 2. Cut three antibodies. Each tip fits one notch.

setup.art: A fourth germ with a slightly different triangle notch, and the old antibody tip not quite fitting.
setup.caption: 3. Make a changed germ. See if the old antibody still fits.

flow.do: A grown-up helps cut three germs from card. Each is a card about 6 by 6 centimetres with a notch on one edge. The notches are a triangle, a half circle and a square. Cut three Y-shaped antibodies, each with a tip that fits one notch. Colour each pair the same colour on the back.
flow.say: These cards are germs. Each has a different notch. These Y shapes are antibodies. Each has a tip that fits one notch. Can you match all three?
flow.kid: Cut three germs with different notches. Cut three Y shapes with matching tips. Match them.

ask.q: Can one antibody fit all three germs? Why or why not?
good: No, each tip fits only one notch.
No, the shapes are different.
Only the one that matches.

flow.parent: Cut the antibody tip first as a small triangle point, then trace the tip onto the edge of the germ card and cut that notch, so the pair fits snugly. Use scissors, not a craft knife. With 2 to 4 children, each child cuts one pair and swaps with another to test the fit.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paper keys. You make three germs and three antibodies, and match them.

flow.do: Now make a fourth germ. Copy the triangle germ, but cut the notch a little wider or at a slightly different angle. Try the triangle antibody on the new germ. See whether it fits.
flow.say: Now the germ changes a little, as flu viruses do. Make a fourth germ like the triangle one, but with a slightly different notch. Does the old antibody still fit?
flow.kid: Make a fourth germ. Change the notch a little. Does the old antibody still fit?

ask.q: What happens to the old antibody when the germ changes a little?
good: It does not fit well.
It slips off.
It does not hold on tight.

flow.parent: A small change makes the old tip fit loosely or not at all. That is how a flu virus can slip past last year's memory. It also means a new antibody is needed, and so a new vaccine.

check.q: The changed germ does not fit the old antibody well. What does this show about the flu?
options: Last year's memory fits a changed flu virus less well, so the vaccine is updated
Flu viruses never change
Antibodies change to match the germ
check.why: Flu viruses slowly change their outer shapes. Old antibodies fit the changed virus less well. That is why the flu vaccine is updated. Antibodies do not change shape to match. A different B cell has to be selected.

flow.context: In this step, you change a germ's shape and see whether the old antibody fits. This shows why flu vaccines are updated.

flow.do: Ask your child to cut a new antibody that fits the changed germ. Ask: in the body, who makes the new antibody? Draw all four pairs and label which is which.
flow.say: Cut a new antibody that fits the changed germ. In a real body, nobody cuts it. Where do you think a fitting one comes from?
flow.kid: Cut a new antibody for the changed germ. Where do you think a real body gets one?

ask.q: In the body, where does the new antibody come from?
good: A B cell that happens to fit.
It was made before.
The body has many B cells with different shapes.

flow.think: In the Key Shop test, nobody made the key after the germ arrived. What did that test show?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the body already holds many different B cells, and one of them may happen to fit the changed germ. If the fit is poor, it may take several days. After they have said what they think, link it back to the Key Shop test.
flow.context: This is the last step of Paper keys. You cut a new antibody and think about where a real body gets one.

projects.title: The long fight against smallpox: a timeline poster

materials.item: a large sheet of chart paper or four A4 sheets taped together
markers, coloured pencils and a ruler
glue and scissors
the timeline facts in the first step

schedule.what: Read the timeline facts. Draw the line on the poster. Write and draw the first four events.
Finish the other events. Add a drawing of the key idea. Show the poster to someone and explain it.

projects.record: Make the poster. On the back, write one sentence that says why smallpox could be stopped, and one that says what you would ask Sarah Nelmes.
projects.context: In this project, you make a timeline poster of how people fought smallpox, from the old ways to the day it was gone. You use what you now know about memory cells.

setup.art: A long sheet of paper with a straight line drawn across the middle and years marked along it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a long line. Mark the years along it.

setup.art: A poster with small boxes along the line, each holding a picture and one sentence.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a small picture and write one sentence for each event.

setup.art: A finished poster with a child pointing to the last box showing a world with no smallpox.
setup.caption: 3. Show your poster to someone and explain it.

flow.do: Read the facts to your child. Smallpox was a deadly illness for thousands of years. Before 1700, people in parts of India, China, Africa and Turkey protected children by variolation, a small dose of real smallpox. 1718: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had her son variolated in Constantinople. 1774: a farmer, Benjamin Jesty, protected his family with cowpox. 1796: Edward Jenner and Sarah Nelmes. 1802: vaccination reached India. 1975: India's last case. 1980: smallpox declared gone from the world.
flow.say: Here is the story in dates. We will put these on a poster. Which ones surprise you? Which would you like to draw?
flow.kid: Here are the dates. Pick the ones you like. We will draw them.

ask.q: Which date surprises you the most? Why?
good: That people used real smallpox on purpose.
That a farmer did it before Jenner.
That it is completely gone.

flow.parent: Check the dates against a source before printing the poster for others. Variolation was widespread but not the same everywhere. Smallpox is the only human illness that has been completely wiped out so far.
flow.context: This is the first step of the smallpox timeline. You read the dates and pick which events to draw.

flow.do: Draw a line across the poster. Mark the dates in order. Draw a small picture and write one sentence for each event. Use plain words. Start with the first four dates today.
flow.say: Draw the line first. Mark the dates in order. For each, draw a small picture and write one sentence. Use words that a friend your age would understand.
flow.kid: Draw a long line. Mark the dates. Draw a small picture for each. Write one sentence.
flow.parent: Help with the spacing. The dates are not evenly spread. A broken line can show a long gap. Ask how the poster would look if all dates were evenly spaced. With 2 to 4 children, share the events between them and join the strips on one poster.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the timeline and the first events.

flow.do: Finish the rest of the dates. Draw in one corner how a vaccine works, using what you know about memory cells. Write one sentence that says why smallpox could be stopped. Show the poster to someone and explain it.
flow.say: Finish the dates. In one corner, draw how a vaccine works, with memory cells. Then explain your poster to someone at home. Why do you think smallpox could be stopped completely?
flow.kid: Finish the dates. Draw how a vaccine works in a corner. Explain your poster to someone.

ask.q: Why do you think smallpox could be stopped completely?
good: Everyone could be protected.
A vaccine worked well.
It only lived in people.

flow.think: Smallpox only lived in people, and it was easy to spot. Why would those two things help?
flow.parent: Strong answers say that smallpox only infected people, showed clear spots so cases could be found, and the vaccine gave strong memory. Teams went everywhere, found each case, and vaccinated the people around it. The cases ran out of paths.
flow.context: This is the last step of the smallpox timeline. You finish the poster and explain why smallpox could be stopped.

challenges.title: The cold box: carry vaccines to a village
challenges.problem: Most vaccines must be kept cool, at about 2 to 8 degrees. If they get warm, they stop working. If they freeze, many are ruined too. A health worker must carry vaccines for four hours, without a fridge. Design a box that keeps a bottle cool but not frozen.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
The bottle of water must start cool from the fridge.
Nothing in the box may freeze the bottle.
The box must be easy to carry.
You must test your design for at least three hours and check the bottle.
materials: three identical bottles of water kept in the fridge overnight
a thermocol box, a steel tiffin box or a lunch box with a lid
a frozen water bottle or an ice pack
a kitchen thermometer, if you have one (a fever thermometer cannot read cold temperatures)
general: Wrap the bottle in a towel and put it in a lid-closed box.
Pack newspaper around the bottle to slow warm air.
Put a frozen bottle beside the water bottle, with a cloth between them so they do not touch.
creative: Put the bottle inside a smaller box, inside a bigger box, with newspaper between them.
Wrap the frozen bottle in cloth so it melts slowly, and tuck it on top.
Use a thermocol box from a delivery, and line it with aluminium foil, shiny side in, to reflect heat.
challenges.your_turn: Test three ways to keep a bottle cool for three hours. Check each bottle with a thermometer or by touch. Pick the best. Then say what would happen if the frozen bottle touched the vaccine.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about vaccines. You keep a bottle cool for three hours without a fridge, as health workers must do on long journeys.

setup.art: Three bottles on a table: one bare, one wrapped in a towel, and one in a closed box with newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Set up three ways to keep a bottle cool.

setup.art: The three bottles in a warm room with a clock showing the time and a note reading start.
setup.caption: 2. Leave them in a warm room for three hours.

setup.art: A hand touching each bottle, with a thermometer beside it and a table of notes.
setup.caption: 3. Check each bottle by touch or with a thermometer.

flow.do: Take three bottles from the fridge. Leave one bare on the table. Wrap one in a towel. Put one in a closed box with newspaper packed around it. Write the time. If you have a thermometer, write each bottle's temperature.
flow.say: These three bottles are as cool as a vaccine should be. We will leave them in the warm room for three hours. Which do you think will stay coolest? Why?
flow.kid: Take three cool bottles. Leave one bare, wrap one in a towel, and pack one in a box. Guess which stays coolest.

ask.q: Which bottle do you think will stay coolest? Why?
good: The one in the box, because the box stops warm air.
The one in the towel.
The bare one will warm the fastest.

flow.parent: Use bottles of the same size and start. If you have a thermometer, check a bottle's temperature in the fridge. Leave them out of the sun.
flow.context: This is the first step of the cold box challenge. You set up three ways to keep a bottle cool.

flow.do: After three hours, check each bottle by touch, and with a thermometer if you have one. For a fair touch test, keep one extra bottle in the fridge as a reference. Ask a sibling or parent to hand you the bottles with your eyes closed, and rank them from coldest to warmest. Write down which is coolest.
flow.say: Three hours have passed. Which bottle feels coolest? Which has warmed most? What does that tell you about the box?
flow.kid: Check each bottle. Which is coolest? Which is warmest?
flow.parent: The bare bottle should be warmest. The boxed bottle is usually coolest, but after three hours without ice every bottle will have warmed above the 2 to 8 degrees a vaccine needs, and only the frozen pack can hold it that cool. If you have a frozen pack, keep it from touching the bottle. A real vaccine must not freeze. Touch is not exact, so write what you felt and say so if two bottles felt the same. With 2 to 4 children, one sets up, one hands over the bottles, and one writes the ranking.

check.q: Why must the frozen pack not touch a vaccine?
options: Freezing can ruin many vaccines
Ice makes vaccines too hard to inject
A frozen pack is too heavy
check.why: Many vaccines are damaged by freezing, just as by heat. They must stay between about 2 and 8 degrees. That is why health workers put a cloth or a divider between ice packs and vaccines.

flow.context: In this step, you check which design kept the bottle cool. You also think about why vaccines must not freeze.

flow.do: Design your own best box using what you learned. Test it for three hours with a bottle from the fridge. Check it afterwards by touch or with a thermometer. Draw the design, and say why it worked.
flow.say: Now design your best box. What did you learn from the first test? Build it, test it for three hours, and check the bottle.
flow.kid: Design your best box. Test it for three hours. Check the bottle.
flow.think: Why does it matter that a vaccine arrives cool, if the germ is the same?
flow.parent: In India, health workers carry vaccines in insulated vaccine carriers with ice packs, and use a cold chain of fridges from the factory to the clinic. The cold chain is one of the hardest parts of vaccination.
flow.context: This is the last step of the cold box challenge. You build your best box and test it.

challenges.safety: Use plastic bottles, not glass. Keep the boxes out of the sun and away from the stove.

challenges.title: The second dose poster: explain it without words
challenges.problem: A health worker visits a village to remind families about the second dose of a vaccine. Many families have never heard of memory cells. Design a one-page picture that explains why the second dose is needed, using as few words as you can.
constraints: Use no more than 20 words on the page.
The picture must make sense to someone who cannot read.
It must be correct: do not say a vaccine makes the child ill.
You must test it on two people and change it once.
materials: two people to test it on
general: Draw a child with a little shield, then the same child with a bigger shield after the second dose.
Draw a ladder with the first dose as the first step, and the second dose as the second step.
Draw a memory cell as a small figure holding a picture of the germ, getting a reminder.
creative: Draw a lamp that glows dim after the first dose, and bright after the second.
Show a team of defenders: a few after one dose, many after two.
Show a calendar with two ticks and a smiling child beside it.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your poster. Show it to two people and ask them to say what it means, in their own words. Do not explain it first. Change it once, using what they said.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about explaining science. You make a picture that helps a family understand why a second dose matters.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a rough sketch of a child with one small shield and then a bigger shield.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch your first idea.

setup.art: A child showing a drawing to an older woman who points at it and speaks.
setup.caption: 2. Show it to someone. Ask them what it means.

setup.art: The same drawing with a new part added, and the older woman nodding.
setup.caption: 3. Change it, using what they said.

flow.do: Ask your child to say the idea in one sentence first. The second dose reminds the body, so the memory is stronger. Then sketch two or three ideas. Choose one.
flow.say: Say the idea in one sentence first. The second dose reminds the body. Now sketch two or three ways to draw it, with no words. Choose the clearest.
flow.kid: Say the idea in one sentence. Sketch two ways to draw it. Choose the clearest.

ask.q: What is the one idea your picture must show?
good: The second dose makes the memory stronger.
The second dose reminds the body.
One dose is a start, and two is stronger.

flow.parent: Many children show a bigger shield, a taller bar or more defenders. All are fine. Help them keep it simple.
flow.context: This is the first step of the second dose poster. You find the idea and sketch ways to show it.

flow.do: Draw the poster neatly in colour with no more than 20 words. Show it to two people. Do not explain it. Ask them to say what it means. Write what they say.
flow.say: Draw your best idea in colour. Then show it to two people. Do not explain. Ask them: what does this say? Write down what they tell you.
flow.kid: Draw your poster in colour. Show it to two people. Ask what it means.

ask.q: Did they understand it? What did they say?
good: Yes, they got the main idea.
They understood part of it.
They thought it meant something else.

flow.parent: If a person says the vaccine makes the child ill, or that the second dose is a punishment, that means the picture needs changing. Thank them for their honest answer.

check.q: A tester says the picture shows the child getting ill after the vaccine. What should you do?
options: Change the picture, because it tells the wrong idea
Tell the tester they are wrong and keep it
Add more words to scare people
check.why: If a viewer takes away the wrong idea, the picture needs to change. The test is not a mistake of the viewer. It shows what the picture says. A good poster is one that people understand correctly the first time.

flow.context: In this step, you draw your poster and test it on two people.

flow.do: Change the poster once, using what the people said. Ask your child to explain what they changed and why. Display the poster.
flow.say: What did your testers tell you? What did you change? Why? Put the poster up where others can see it.
flow.kid: Change the poster using what people said. Tell us what you changed.
flow.think: A health worker often has to explain science without a lab or a screen. What makes an explanation work?
flow.parent: A good answer names what was misunderstood and how the new picture fixes it. Improving after testing is what scientists and designers do.
flow.context: This is the last step of the second dose poster. You change the poster after testing and say what you changed.

items.p: Which defence reacts within minutes, in much the same way to almost every germ?
opts: The quick defence
The defence that learns
Memory cells
items.why: The quick defence is the one you are born with. It includes skin, tears and white blood cells that eat germs. It is fast but does not tell germs apart well. The defence that learns takes days the first time.

items.p: The quick defence remembers a germ so it can act faster next time.
items.why: False. The quick defence reacts the same way every time. Only the defence that learns, with its memory cells, remembers a germ.

items.p: A tiny Y-shaped protein that fits one germ shape is called an ____.
items.why: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein. Its tips fit one antigen, like a key in a lock. Each kind of antibody fits only one shape.

items.p: Match each part of the defence that learns to its job.
pairs: destroys body cells with a virus hidden inside
a small knot where immune cells meet and multiply
stays after a fight and acts fast next time
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: B cells make antibodies. Killer T cells find cells with a virus inside. Lymph nodes are meeting places. Memory cells stay for years and respond fast.

items.p: Sort each one by which defence does it.
items: a killer T cell finding a virus
items.a: as given
items.why: The quick defence is always ready and the same for every germ. The defence that learns uses antibodies, T cells and memory.

items.p: Why does the defence that learns take about a week the first time a germ arrives?
opts: It has to find and multiply the one cell that fits that germ
It waits for the germ to die first
It has to be taught by a doctor
items.why: The body already holds many cells, but only a few fit a new germ. Those few must divide until there are enough to fight. That takes days. Memory cells make it faster next time.

items.p: An antibody against measles will also stick to a flu virus.
items.why: False. An antibody fits one shape. A measles antibody does not fit a flu virus, so a different antibody is needed.

items.p: A friend asks why most people only get chickenpox once. Explain it in two or three sentences.
items.a: The first time, the body finds the cells that fit the virus and some stay behind as memory cells. If the virus returns, the memory cells act in a few days, before it can make you ill.
items.why: A strong answer says that memory cells stay after the first illness and make the second response fast. It may add that the first response is slow.

items.p: Put these in order, for what happens when a germ meets a body for the first time.
a: The germ meets the one B cell whose antibody fits
That B cell splits into many copies
The copies make lots of antibodies
A few cells stay behind as memory cells
items.why: The germ comes first. It picks a matching cell. That cell copies itself, the copies fight, and a few remain as memory.

items.p: What does a vaccine do?
opts: It shows the body a safe version of a germ, so memory cells are made before the real germ arrives
It kills every germ in the body for ever
It gives the body the antibodies ready-made, to use up
items.why: A vaccine does the slow first lesson in a safe way. B cells and T cells find the safe version, multiply, and leave memory cells behind.

items.p: Kavya's card shows polio drops 3 times, measles and rubella 2 times and one booster. How many doses are there in all?
items.why: 3 plus 2 plus 1 is 6. Some vaccines are given in more than one dose so the memory is stronger.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Skin, tears, mucus, memory cell.
items.a: Memory cell, because it belongs to the defence that learns. The other three are walls that are always there, in the quick defence.
items.why: Skin, tears and mucus work the same against all germs. A memory cell remembers one germ.

items.p: Draw an antibody holding on to the spike of a germ. Show how the shapes fit.
items.a: A Y-shaped antibody with one tip fitting into a notch or a spike on a round germ.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the tip of the Y fitting the shape on the germ exactly, and not just touching.

items.p: A family is not sure about taking a child for a vaccine.

views.says: I have seen what measles does. The vaccine gives the memory without the illness, and a sore arm for a day is a small price.
My child is so small. I want to understand what goes in, and what might go wrong, before I agree.
I remember when polio left children unable to walk. I am glad no child I know has that now.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What questions would you want answered before you decided?
items.a: Any view with a reason is fine. A strong answer asks real questions, such as what is in the vaccine, how safe it is, and what the illness can do.
items.why: Vaccines are one place where evidence and fear meet. A good decision uses the evidence and also listens to the worry.

items.p: A child has a sore arm and a mild fever the day after a vaccine. What is the best explanation?
opts: The immune system is responding, which is expected
The vaccine has given the child the illness
The vaccine has failed
items.why: A sore arm or a low fever shows the immune system at work. It is usually mild and short. A high fever, trouble breathing or a rash needs a doctor.

items.p: A fever after a vaccine always means something has gone wrong.
items.why: False. A mild fever can be the immune system at work. A fever that is high or that lasts needs a doctor.

items.p: How many kinds of antibody does one B cell make?
opts: One kind
As many as there are germs
Three kinds
items.why: Each B cell makes only one kind of antibody. That is why the body needs millions of different B cells, each ready for a different shape.

items.p: Why does the body need killer T cells as well as antibodies?
opts: Viruses hide inside body cells, where antibodies cannot reach
Antibodies are too slow
Killer T cells make antibodies
items.why: Antibodies work on germs floating outside cells. A virus inside a cell is out of their reach. Killer T cells find and destroy the cell with the virus hidden in it.

items.p: The fluid that drains from your tissues, flows through the nodes and returns to your blood is called ____.
items.why: Lymph carries bits of whatever is in the tissues, including germ pieces, through lymph nodes. In the nodes, immune cells can meet them.

items.p: Match each kind of vaccine to what it shows the body.
pairs: a germ made too weak to make you ill
a harmless form of a germ's poison
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: All four show the immune system an antigen without the real illness. B cells and T cells then make memory cells.

items.p: Put these in order, for how a vaccine protects someone.
a: A vaccine shows the body a safe antigen
Scout cells carry a piece to a lymph node
B cells and T cells that fit multiply
The real germ arrives and is stopped fast
items.why: The vaccine comes first, and the immune cells do their work. Memory cells wait for the real germ, and then act quickly.

items.p: A chosen B cell splits in two every 8 hours. Starting with 1 cell, how many cells are there after 24 hours?
items.why: In 24 hours there are three splits of 8 hours. 1 becomes 2, then 4, then 8.

items.p: Every B cell is made after a germ arrives.
items.why: False. The body makes B cells with many different shapes before any germ arrives. The germ only picks one that fits.

items.p: One scientist says a germ teaches the body how to make an antibody. Another says the germ only picks one that is already there. Use the Key Shop test to say which is better supported.
items.a: The germ picks one that is already there. In the Key Shop test, nobody shaped a key for the germ. We made random keys, and one matched by chance. The more shapes were possible, the more keys we needed.
items.why: A strong answer uses the test as evidence. It says the cells were made without knowing the germ, so the germ chose, and did not teach.

items.p: A school has some children who cannot be vaccinated because of a health condition.

views.says: These children rely on everyone else being protected. High vaccination in the school keeps the germ from reaching them.

views.who: A parent who is unsure (an imagined view)
views.says: I worry about giving my own child something I do not fully understand, even if it helps others.

views.who: A child with a weak immune system (an imagined view)
views.says: I cannot choose to be vaccinated. I depend on my friends being protected.

items.ask: Whose view helps you most to decide what a school should do? What would you want to know first?
items.a: Any view with a reason is fine. A strong answer weighs the child who cannot be vaccinated against the worry of the unsure parent, and asks for facts.
items.why: Herd protection means one family's choice affects others. A good answer takes both the evidence and the worry seriously.

items.p: Why is a tiny baby safer when the people around her are all protected?
opts: The germ finds fewer people to spread through, so it rarely reaches her
The baby gets their antibodies through the air
Protected people cannot carry any germs at all
items.why: A germ needs a path from person to person. When most people are protected, the germ stops before it gets to the baby. That is herd protection.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Chickenpox, measles, a cold, mumps.
items.a: A cold, because hundreds of different viruses cause colds, so memory for one does not protect against the next. The other three are each caused by one virus.
items.why: Memory helps most when the germ stays the same. Colds change because many viruses cause them.

items.p: Draw a graph with two lines. One shows antibodies during a first infection. The other shows antibodies during a second infection with the same germ.
items.a: The first line rises slowly over about a week or more to a low peak. The second line rises in two to four days to a much higher peak.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the second line rising earlier and higher than the first, because memory cells act at once.

items.p: Why must the flu vaccine be updated each year?
opts: Flu viruses slowly change their outer shapes, so last year's memory fits less well
The vaccine wears out in the bottle
Antibodies disappear after a month
items.why: Flu viruses change the shapes on their surface. An old antibody fits a changed virus less well. A new vaccine shows the body the new shapes.

items.p: A stronger immune system is always better.
items.why: False. An overactive immune system causes allergies, and in some people attacks the body's own cells. A healthy immune system is balanced.

items.p: A body builds billions of different antibody shapes by shuffling and joining a few hundred gene ____.
items.why: A B cell picks one piece from each of three lists and joins them, and adds a few random letters at the joins. A small set of pieces makes billions of shapes.

items.p: A vaccine protects a child who was vaccinated. Explain how it can also protect a child who was never vaccinated.
items.a: If many people are protected, the germ cannot find enough people to spread through. A child who was not vaccinated is less likely to meet the germ, because it stops at the protected people around her.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of paths. Protected people block paths, and so the germ rarely reaches unprotected people.

items.p: A scientist finds that a single cell makes only one kind of antibody, before meeting any germ. Which idea does this support?
opts: The germ picks a ready-made cell and does not shape the antibody
The germ shapes the antibody like clay around a coin
Antibodies are not made by cells
items.why: If a cell already makes one fixed kind before any germ arrives, the germ cannot have shaped it. The germ can only find the cell that fits.

items.p: A child tests shields in a grid town but chooses the places herself. What is the problem with her test?
opts: She might choose places that block the germ well, so the number of shields is not the only change
Choosing is always more fair than drawing
Shields do not matter in a grid
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. If she picks smart places, then the places and the number both change. Drawing from a bowl keeps the places random.

items.p: The first vaccine test was done on a healthy eight-year-old boy, and then he was exposed to smallpox. Why would this not be allowed today? Describe how a careful test would be done instead.
items.a: Today we do not deliberately expose healthy children to a deadly illness. A careful test would first be done in a lab and then on small groups of adults who agree, with doctors watching and the right to leave. Then it would be tested on larger groups, always with checks and agreement.
items.why: A strong answer names consent and safety, and describes testing in steps from small to large. Jenner did not know how to do this, and the world has learned since.

items.p: A germ whose outer shape changes can slip past old ____.
items.why: Memory cells and antibodies fit a germ's old shape. If the shape changes, the fit is poor, and the germ gets past.

items.p: Match each problem to what is happening in the body.
pairs: the defence reacts strongly to something harmless
the defence attacks the body's own cells
some parts of the defence are missing or not working
the germ's shape changes, so old memory fits less well
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each is a different way the defence can fall short. Three come from the body, and one comes from the germ.

items.p: Sort each one by whether memory helps.
items: a brand-new type of flu virus
a cold from a different cold virus
a tetanus booster ten years later
a germ whose shape changes each month
items.a: as given
items.why: Memory works when the germ stays the same, or when a booster reminds the memory cells. It works less when the germ changes or is a different germ.

items.p: In an unprotected town, a sick person would pass a germ to 4 other people. Out of every 4 people, how many must be protected so that a sick person passes it on to only 1 person?
items.a: 3 out of every 4
items.why: If 3 of the 4 people are protected, only 1 can catch it. So a sick person passes it on to 1 person, and the germ no longer grows. That is 3 out of 4, or 75 out of 100.

items.p: An unprotected person is safer in a town where most people are protected than in a town where few are.
items.why: True. In a town with many protected people, a germ finds few paths and rarely reaches the unprotected person.

items.p: A vaccine has a small risk for each person, and protects others in the town.

views.says: The risk to each person is very small, and the protection for the whole town is large. We should encourage everyone to take it.
I accept a small risk for my own child. I want to be told clearly what the risk is and be given a choice.
A choice that affects others is not only private. But people trust a system more when it explains and listens.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What would make you trust a vaccine?
items.a: Any view with a reason is fine. A strong answer weighs the small risk against the larger benefit and says how trust could be built.
items.why: Herd protection joins one person's choice to everyone's safety. Good decisions explain the evidence and listen.

items.p: Compare the Key Shop test with natural selection among animals in a forest. What is the same, and what is different?
items.a: Both begin with many different forms made without knowing what will be needed. In the forest, the surroundings keep the animals that fit. In the body, the germ keeps the cell that fits. The difference is speed and place: in the body it takes days and happens inside one body, and in a forest it takes many lifetimes.
items.why: A strong answer says that in both cases the variety exists first and something in the surroundings picks. It notes that the body does it in days, not generations.

items.p: Which is not a way to make a vaccine? A weakened germ, a killed germ, a harmless form of a poison, a germ made stronger.
items.a: A germ made stronger, because vaccines use safer versions of a germ, not stronger ones.
items.why: A vaccine must teach the immune system without causing the illness. It uses weakened or killed germs, a piece of a germ, or a harmless form of a poison.

items.p: Draw a town where most houses have a shield and a few do not. Show the germ's path stopping at the shields.
items.a: A grid of houses, most with shield marks, a few without, and arrows showing the germ spreading from one sick house and stopping at the shields.
items.why: A strong drawing shows unshielded houses surrounded by shields, with no arrow reaching them.

items.p: In the Spread and Shield test, one group had 16 shields but 9 sick squares. Which is the best next step?
opts: Run the town again several times, since chance can change one result
Decide that shields do not work
Choose the shield squares by hand next time
items.why: Dice are random, so one run can be unusual. Repeating the town and adding up the results shows the pattern. Choosing squares by hand would stop the test being fair.

items.p: Put these in order, for what happens the second time a known germ arrives.
a: Antibodies appear within two to four days
The germ is stopped before illness
items.why: Memory cells are already waiting, so they act at once. This is much faster than the first meeting, when the matching cell had to be found.

items.p: A vaccine made and tested in one country works in exactly the same way in every country.
items.why: False. Differences such as nutrition, gut infections and other germs can change how well some vaccines work. This is why scientists, such as Gagandeep Kang, test vaccines in the places where they will be used.

items.p: There is a vaccine for measles, but not one for the common cold. Give two reasons why a cold vaccine is much harder to make.
items.a: More than 200 different viruses cause colds, so one vaccine would have to fit many shapes. Cold viruses also change over time, so the memory would fit less well.
items.why: A strong answer names the number of different viruses and their changing shapes. Both make a single memory hard to use.

quiz.p: Which is true of the quick defence?
opts: It acts within minutes or hours, and in much the same way against most germs
It makes a different antibody for each germ
It remembers a germ for years
quiz.why: The quick defence is always ready and does not tell germs apart well. Antibodies and memory belong to the defence that learns.

quiz.p: Why does an antibody for one germ not work against a different germ?
opts: Its shape fits one antigen only, like a key in one lock
Antibodies are too slow
Different germs do not have shapes
quiz.why: An antibody's tip fits one shape. A different germ has a different shape, so a different antibody is needed.

quiz.p: In the Key Shop test, the average number of cells rose when each code had more flips. What does this show about a body's defender cells?
opts: The more shapes are possible, the more random cells are needed to find a match
More flips make the germ weaker
A matching cell is always found on the first try
quiz.why: More flips mean more possible shapes, and the matching one is rarer. A real body deals with this by making huge numbers of cells with many different shapes.

quiz.p: A child meets measles for the second time. Why is she far less likely to get ill than the first time?
opts: Memory cells recognise the germ and act within days
The germ gets weaker each time
Her skin has become thicker
quiz.why: After the first meeting, memory cells stay. When the germ returns they multiply and make antibodies very fast, before the germ can make her ill.

quiz.p: What does a vaccine do for a child who has never met the real germ?
opts: It starts the slow first lesson safely, so memory cells are ready
It gives the child the full illness in a mild form
It makes the skin harder for germs to pass
quiz.why: A vaccine shows the immune system a safe version of the germ. The matching cells multiply, and memory cells stay for later.

quiz.p: Why might a child need a booster dose of a vaccine?
opts: The memory can fade over time, and an extra dose strengthens it
The first dose was a mistake
A booster makes the vaccine cheaper
quiz.why: For some germs, the antibodies slowly fall over the years. A booster reminds the memory cells and brings the protection back up.

quiz.p: When most people in a town are protected, even a few people who are not protected are safer.
quiz.why: True. The germ has fewer paths to reach them. This is herd protection.

opts: The immune system reacts strongly to something harmless, such as pollen
A germ that lives in the nose
A kind of vaccine
quiz.why: In an allergy, the defence treats a harmless thing as if it were a germ. That causes sneezing, itching or a rash.

quiz.p: Why can a person catch a cold many times in a life, though memory cells exist?
opts: Many different viruses cause colds, so memory for one does not fit the next
Memory cells only last a week
Colds are not caused by germs
quiz.why: More than 200 different viruses cause colds. Memory for one does not fit another. Chickenpox is one virus, so memory helps for life.

quiz.p: How does a body get an antibody for a germ it has never met before?
opts: It already holds many B cells with different shapes, and one of them fits
It copies the shape of the germ at once
A doctor adds the antibody to the blood
quiz.why: B cells with many different shapes are made before any germ arrives. The germ finds the one that fits, and that one multiplies. This is clonal selection.

applications: Vaccines for babies and children, such as polio drops, measles and rubella, protect them before they meet the real germs.
Booster doses, such as the extra tetanus dose for older children, bring memory back up.
Each year, scientists update the flu vaccine to match the viruses that are going around.
Doctors give people with a deep cut an extra tetanus dose, because the bacteria that cause tetanus can live in soil and rust.
Blood tests that look for antibodies show whether someone has been protected by a vaccine or has had an illness.
Cold chains of fridges, ice boxes and vaccine carriers keep vaccines cool all the way to remote villages.
Community health workers, called ASHA workers in India, visit homes to remind families about vaccine days.
Doctors treat allergies by finding what the body reacts to, and sometimes by giving tiny, careful doses to teach the body to tolerate it.
Scientists make antibodies in the lab, using the shapes that fit a germ, to treat some illnesses.
Rotavac, a vaccine against a cause of severe diarrhoea in children, was developed in India and tested here, so that it works for children here.

open_questions.q: Why do some memories last for life while others fade after a few years?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists see that memory for measles lasts for decades and memory for some other germs fades. They do not fully know why.

open_questions.q: Why does the same germ make one person very ill and another person hardly ill at all?
open_questions.why_open: Age, genes, earlier illnesses, nutrition and luck all play a part, but nobody can yet predict exactly how one person's body will react.

open_questions.q: Why does the defence sometimes attack the body's own cells?
open_questions.why_open: In many autoimmune illnesses, scientists know which cells are attacked, but not always what started the mistake.

open_questions.q: Could we make one vaccine that protects against all flu viruses, or all cold viruses?
open_questions.why_open: Researchers are trying to find shapes that stay the same across many strains. They have not yet succeeded.

open_questions.q: How do the immune system and the brain talk to each other?
open_questions.why_open: Signals pass between them, and sleep and stress change how the defence works, but the details are still being found.

open_questions.q: Are there more ways to remember than memory cells?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists have found that even the quick defence can change after a first meeting with a germ. They call this trained immunity, and are still working out how much it matters.

maths.problem: In the Key Shop test, one family needed these numbers of cells in six rounds with three flips: 6, 12, 3, 9, 15 and 5. They also did four more rounds: 4, 10, 7 and 9. What was the average number of cells over all ten rounds?
maths.explain: Add all ten numbers: 6 plus 12 is 18, plus 3 is 21, plus 9 is 30, plus 15 is 45, plus 5 is 50, plus 4 is 54, plus 10 is 64, plus 7 is 71, plus 9 is 80. Divide 80 by 10 to get 8. Three flips give 8 shapes, so about 8 cells are needed on average.
maths.context: In the Key Shop test, you count how many random cells you need until one matches the germ, over several rounds.
maths.why_maths: One round can be lucky or unlucky. The average of many rounds shows the pattern, which is what the number of shapes predicts.

maths.problem: A code of 2 coin flips gives 4 shapes. A code of 3 flips gives 8 shapes. A code of 4 flips gives 16 shapes. How many shapes would a code of 8 flips give? Explain how you know.
maths.explain: Each extra flip doubles the number of shapes. 16 doubled is 32 for 5 flips, then 64, then 128, then 256 for 8 flips.
maths.context: In the Key Shop test, each extra flip in the code made the number of shapes grow.
maths.why_maths: Spotting a doubling pattern lets you work out big numbers without flipping a coin 8 times.

maths.problem: A code of 10 flips gives 1,024 shapes. A code of 20 flips gives about 1,000,000 shapes. About how many shapes would a code of 30 flips give?
maths.explain: Ten more flips multiplies the shapes by about 1,000, because 10 flips make about 1,000 shapes. So 20 flips is about a million, and 30 flips is about a thousand million, which is a billion. A real body makes billions of antibody shapes.
maths.context: Your body makes billions of different antibody shapes, which is a very large number.
maths.why_maths: Doubling many times makes numbers that are too big to imagine. Seeing how fast they grow shows how a body can hold so many shapes.

maths.problem: A germ doubles in number every 4 hours. A chosen B cell doubles every 8 hours. Both start with 1. After 48 hours, how many germs and how many B cells are there? Which is bigger? Why does the body need help from memory cells?
maths.answer: 4,096 germs and 64 B cells. The germs are far more. Memory cells start with many cells already made.
maths.explain: In 48 hours, the germ doubles 12 times, because 48 divided by 4 is 12. Twelve doublings from 1 make 4,096. The B cell doubles 6 times, because 48 divided by 8 is 6. Six doublings make 64. The germs win at first. That is why you can be ill the first time. With memory, the body starts with many more cells, so it can win.
maths.context: The first time a germ arrives, the body must find and multiply the one cell that fits, while the germ is also multiplying.
maths.why_maths: Doubling shows why a small head start matters. Comparing the two growth rates explains why the first meeting is risky and the second is not.

maths.problem: In the Spread and Shield test, a town has 25 squares. In town C, 16 squares have a shield and 3 got sick. What fraction of the town is shielded? What percent is that?
maths.answer: 16 out of 25, which is 64 out of 100, or 64 percent.
maths.explain: 16 out of 25 is the same as 64 out of 100, because multiplying both numbers by 4 gives 64 and 100. So 64 percent of the town was shielded. The 3 sick squares were a small share of the 9 that had no shield.
maths.context: In the Spread and Shield test, you shield some of the 25 squares and count how many get sick.
maths.why_maths: Percent lets you compare towns of different sizes. A real town of thousands can be compared with your 25 squares.

maths.problem: In the word puzzle, Meenakshi took 150 seconds the first time and 60 seconds the second time. How many seconds faster was the second time? How many times as fast was it?
maths.answer: 90 seconds faster. 2 and a half times as fast.
maths.explain: 150 take away 60 is 90 seconds. To compare, divide 150 by 60, which is 2 and a half. The second time was 2 and a half times as fast, like memory cells acting faster on a second meeting.
maths.context: In the word puzzle, you time yourself solving the same words twice.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting tells you how much time was saved. Dividing tells you how many times faster, which is a better way to compare.

how_we_found_out.story: For many years, scientists believed that antibodies were moulded around germs, like clay pressed around a coin. In 1940, the chemist Linus Pauling gave this idea a clear form. It explained how a body could make a fitting antibody for almost anything. But in 1955, Niels Jerne suggested the opposite. He said the body already holds many kinds of antibodies, and a germ only finds the one that fits. In 1957, Macfarlane Burnet added that each cell makes only one kind and copies itself when chosen. In 1958, Gustav Nossal and Joshua Lederberg tested this. They put single cells from a rat into tiny drops. Each cell made only one kind of antibody. The germ had not shaped it. Burnet shared the 1960 Nobel Prize, and Jerne won the Nobel Prize in 1984.
how_we_found_out.who: Linus Pauling, Niels Jerne, Macfarlane Burnet, Gustav Nossal and Joshua Lederberg
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Antibodies are moulded around each germ, like clay around a coin. Nossal and Lederberg's single-cell test showed that each cell makes only one kind before it meets any germ, so the germ picks, and does not shape.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, and checked on paper, but not cooked at home with real children. The Key Shop test needs only a coin. Spread and Shield and Shield the Town were checked by running their dice rules on a computer thousands of times. With no shields the germ reached about 21 of 25 squares on average. With 8 shields it reached about 8, and with 16 shields about 3, with wide ranges, so the steps tell families to repeat a town if chance misleads them. In Shield the Town with 10 shields on a 6 by 6 board, careless placement gave about 10 sick squares and careful placement does better, so 8 or fewer is a fair target. The word puzzle is a model and says so. Cold box: bottles should start cool from the fridge, and a frozen pack must not touch them.
